title: Alabama Data Breach Notification Act
summary: Requires reasonable safeguards, investigation, and notification for qualifying compromises of sensitive identifying information.
scope: Covered entities and third-party agents holding covered information.
rights: Affected residents receive qualifying breach notices.
obligations: Maintain reasonable security measures and investigate potential breaches.
deadlines: Resident notice generally within 45 days of statutory determination/third-party notice; agents notify covered entities within 10 days.
authority: Alabama Attorney General
exemptions: Federal-regulated entities must follow their notice procedures and timely copy the AG when more than 1,000 people are notified. State-regulated procedures must also be at least as thorough as this chapter. Public information and properly protected unreadable information are excluded, subject to compromised-key conditions.
penalties: The AG exclusively enforces statutory civil penalties. Knowing notice violations carry cross-referenced consumer-protection penalties capped at $500,000 per breach; failure to take reasonable notice-compliance action can additionally draw up to $5,000 per day. The AG may recover actual damages for named individuals plus fees and costs. Government entities avoid civil penalties but remain subject to compliance orders. No private cause arises under section 8-19-10; independent rights are preserved.
amendments: The reviewed official agency reproduction credits Act 2018-396 throughout. It does not establish a complete later-session amendment search.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Criminal eavesdropping
summary: Criminalizes intentional device-based eavesdropping on private communications.
scope: Persons using devices to eavesdrop.
rights: Protection against interception without a participant’s consent.
obligations: Obtain legally sufficient consent or identify an applicable statutory exception.
deadlines: Conduct prohibition; no consumer-request deadline.
authority: State and local criminal prosecutors
effective: 1980-01-01 at 12:01 a.m. (Title 13 A commencement under §13 A-1-11)
exemptions: Statutory defenses cover lawful police duties; common-carrier personnel performing necessary service or protecting carrier rights/property; and good-faith reliance on a lawful court order or legislative authorization. Defendant must raise the defense, without shifting the ultimate burden of proof.
penalties: Criminal eavesdropping is a Class A misdemeanor: imprisonment up to one year. General misdemeanor fine is up to $6,000, with an alternative amount up to twice the offender’s pecuniary gain or victim’s loss under section 13A-5-12(a)(4).
amendments: The 2025 statutory reproduction attributes §13A-11-31 solely to 1977 Act 607 §5605, with no subsequent amendment listed for that section. The separate definitions, device-installation and disclosure provisions must be read alongside it. The 2012 SB 53 proposal was postponed rather than enacted; it is not substituted for the statute.

title: Personal Information Protection Act—breach notice
summary: Establishes notice duties following security breaches involving personal information.
scope: Information collectors holding covered personal information.
rights: Qualifying affected consumers receive breach notice.
obligations: Notify affected Alaska residents; substitute notice uses email, website and statewide media when qualifying; notify consumer reporting agencies at 1,000 or more affected persons.
deadlines: Resident notice most expeditious time possible without unreasonable delay, subject to statutory investigation/law-enforcement conditions; no fixed general day count in reviewed guidance.
authority: Alaska Department of Law
exemptions: Official legislative-hosted guidance reviewed is historical; current exemptions require recheck.
penalties: Original §45.48.080: up to $500 per unnotified resident, total $50,000; injunction. Private economic recovery under §45.50.531 limited to $500, and §45.50.537 to actual economic damages.
amendments: Source is 2016 official guidance; current amendments not fully reconciled.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Personal Information Protection Act—record disposal
summary: Requires protected disposal of records containing personal information.
scope: Businesses operating in Alaska or possessing Alaska residents’ covered personal information, including possession for destruction; state/local governmental agencies other than the judicial branch. Disposal includes discarding records and selling, donating or transferring storage media and equipment containing them.
rights: Protection from exposure of discarded personal information.
obligations: Take reasonable measures against unauthorized access or use during disposal. Section 510 identifies unreadable paper destruction, nonpaper erasure/destruction and, after due diligence, a written contract with a record-destruction business as compliance measures. Section 500 limits responsibility after a compliant transfer to such a third party, or after return to the individual concerned.
deadlines: Applies when covered records are disposed of.
authority: Alaska Department of Law
exemptions: Section 540 exempts conflicting federal requirements, compliant GLBA-regulated businesses and businesses subject to and complying with the FCRA disposal requirement. Section 590 excludes judicial-branch agencies and public information voluntarily made public from its defined records.
penalties: Original §§45.48.550–560: knowing violation up to $3,000; injured individual may seek injunction, actual economic damages, court costs and full reasonable attorney fees.
amendments: The 2025 statutory reproduction separately confirms the record-disposal duties and exceptions; it is distinguished from the historical 2016 agency guidance. The official 2026 session-law index was reviewed through November 17, 2026: all 61 linked enacted chapters (1–61) were retrieved as valid PDFs and their complete text searched for AS 45.48, AS 14.03.110, AS 42.20 and related privacy terms. No reference to those target provisions appeared. This establishes the bounded 2026 enacted-text reconciliation for these provisions; it does not describe a pending bill as law or claim an absence of every other Alaska privacy protection.

title: Security system breach notification
summary: Requires investigation and notice of covered computerized-data breaches.
scope: Persons conducting business in Arizona owning, maintaining, or licensing covered computerized information.
rights: Affected individuals receive required breach information.
obligations: Investigate incidents; notify residents; above 1, 000 notify AG, Homeland Security Director, and three largest nationwide reporting agencies.
deadlines: 45 days after breach determination; owner notice by maintainers as soon as practicable; law-enforcement delay allows 45 days after clearance.
authority: Arizona Attorney General
effective: Original 2007-01-01: Act says from and after December 31, 2006; official judiciary legislative summary expressly calls this January 1, 2007.2018 revision 2018-08-03; 2022 chapter 81 amendment 2022-09-24.
exemptions: GLBA-regulated persons and specified HIPAA-compliant entities excluded; reasonable-investigation finding of no actual/likely substantial economic loss can excuse notice.
penalties: Knowing/willful violations: lesser of $10, 000 per affected person or economic loss; $500, 000 aggregate maximum per related breach series.
amendments: 2018 ch 177 revised/renumbered; 2022 ch 81 added Homeland Security Director notice; both enacted texts reviewed.

title: Personal Information Protection Act
summary: Requires reasonable protection of personal information and notice when covered information is compromised.
scope: Entities collecting covered personal information.
rights: Affected individuals receive timely breach notice.
obligations: Use reasonable security practices; report qualifying breaches to Attorney General.
deadlines: Individual notice most expediently possible without unreasonable delay. Above 1,000 affected: AG at individual notice or within 45 days after likely-harm determination, whichever first. Retain determination records five years; supply AG within 30 days of written request.
authority: Arkansas Attorney General
effective: 2005-08-12 (original Act 1526; general effective date, no special clause)
exemptions: Greater-protection state/federal law with at least equally thorough notification may qualify; good-faith employee acquisition and reasonable no-likely-harm findings have conditions.
penalties: Section 4-110-108 authorizes AG action under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Cross-referenced §4-88-113 permits court orders stopping unlawful practices, restitution/damages, civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation, and possible suspension/forfeiture of business authority. Injunction violations have a separate up-to $10,000 penalty per AG action. No automatic private breach remedy is inferred from this AG cross-reference.
amendments: Official AG guidance identifies an amendment requiring AG reporting above 1,000 affected individuals with reasonable likelihood of harm.

title: Public entity security-incident reporting
summary: Requires public-sector security incidents to be reported to the Legislative Auditor.
scope: State entities, political subdivisions and schools. Covered incidents include unauthorized compromise of systems maintained by their contracted service providers; the reporting duty is placed on the public entity.
rights: Public accountability through incident reporting.
obligations: Written initial known-facts report to Legislative Auditor; regular incident updates. Statutory reports/updates are exempt from FOIA as security functions.
deadlines: Initial written known-facts report within five business days after learning of an incident; regular updates until the investigation closes. Auditor reports the incident list to designated legislative committees annually by December 15.
authority: Arkansas Legislative Auditor
effective: 2021-07-28 (Act 260 passed before the extended recess without a special clause; official BLR table confirms the pre-recess general effective date).
exemptions: No general reporting exception stated in Act 260. Incident reports/updates/lists are exempt from public disclosure as security functions under §25-19-105(b)(11); this is confidentiality, not an exemption from reporting.
penalties: Section 10-4-429 contains no fixed fine or express consumer damages award for a late incident report. Separate audit powers permit subpoenaed evidence; noncompliance with an auditor subpoena can lead to circuit-court contempt, and knowing material false sworn testimony can constitute perjury under §10-4-421. Section 10-4-419 requires referral/cooperation concerning apparent criminal offenses. Those consequences require their own predicates; a late report alone is not automatically contempt or perjury.
amendments: 2025 codification credits 2021 Act 260 section 1 and 2023 Act 175 section 2. Current text expressly requires updates until investigation closes. Separate 2025 Act 489 governs the State Cybersecurity Office.

title: Colorado Privacy Act
summary: Creates consumer control over personal data and duties for covered controllers and processors.
scope: 100, 000 Colorado consumers, or 25, 000 plus revenue/discount from data sales; covered nonprofits included.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, and specified profiling.
obligations: Provide notices, safeguards, assessments, sensitive-data consent, and processor contracts.
deadlines: Requests: 45 days, with a justified additional 45 days; universal opt-out recognition began July 1, 2024.
authority: Colorado Attorney General and district attorneys
exemptions: Commercial/employment consumer contexts excluded from general CPA rights; GLBA, specified health, FCRA/FERPA and other data exemptions require application.
penalties: AG/district-attorney-exclusive enforcement; no private CPA action. Original mandatory 60-day cure provision expired Jan 1, 2025; general CCPA remedy amounts need current-code reconciliation.
amendments: 2024 biometric and children’s-data amendments have separate 2025 operative dates; general mandatory cure provision expired Jan 1, 2025.

title: Consumer data security and breach notification
summary: Requires safeguards, proper disposal, investigation, and breach notifications.
scope: Covered holders of Colorado residents’ personal information.
rights: Qualifying residents receive notice of compromised information.
obligations: Investigate suspected breaches; notify AG for 500 or more affected Coloradans.
deadlines: Resident notice without unreasonable delay and within 30 days after determination. AG at 500 or more residents within 30 days; nationwide credit agencies above 1,000 without unreasonable delay.
authority: Colorado Attorney General
enacted: Disposal §6-1-713 added by 2004 HB 1311 §2; notification §6-1-716 added by 2006 HB 1119/chapter 145 §1.2018 HB 1128 amendment approved 2018-05-29.
effective: Original disposal rule 2004-08-04; original breach notification 2006-09-01.2018 security/notification revision 2018-09-01.
exemptions: Documented good-faith finding of no misuse/likely misuse; conditional regulator-compliance provisions. Regulated entities still owe qualifying AG notice and must use the shorter applicable resident-notice period.
penalties: §6-1-716(4) authorizes AG law/equity actions for compliance and direct economic damages for violations of breach, disposal and reasonable-security provisions. This section states no numeric fine; independent Consumer Protection Act penalty predicates require separate analysis.
amendments: Official 2017 code history confirms disposal originated 2004 HB 1311, originally numbered 6-1-712 then renumbered 6-1-713. Notification originated 2006 HB 1119/chapter 145; 2018 chapter 266/HB 1128 expanded security, disposal, notice and AG enforcement. Complete later-session audit remains open.

title: Social Media and the Workplace Act
summary: Limits employer demands for access to personal electronic accounts.
scope: Colorado private enterprises and state/local government employers, their agents and representatives, and employees or applicants. The statutory employer definition excludes corrections departments and state/local law-enforcement agencies.
rights: Refuse covered access demands without retaliation.
obligations: Do not require prohibited credentials, contact-list additions, or privacy-setting changes.
deadlines: Complaint and hearing procedures apply; findings within 30 days after hearing.
authority: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment
exemptions: Employer internal-system nonpersonal accounts; specified securities/financial-compliance investigations based on information received; investigations of unauthorized downloads of employer proprietary or financial data. Consistent personnel policies and existing confidentiality duties remain enforceable.
penalties: Labor Division fine up to $1,000 first offense and $5,000 per subsequent offense.
amendments: The official 2026 Title 8 source note lists the original HB 13-1046, chapter 195 §1, effective May 11, 2013, with no later amendment attributed to §8-2-127 in that compilation.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Connecticut Data Privacy Act
summary: Gives residents personal-data rights and establishes controller/processor duties.
scope: Since July 1, 2026: 35, 000 consumers excluding payment-only processing; or processing sensitive data; or offering personal data for sale, under §42-516.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, third-party-sale information, and covered opt-outs.
obligations: Obtain sensitive-data consent, provide notices, honor opt-outs, and assess covered processing.
deadlines: Requests: 45 days, possible 45-day extension; appeals 60 days.
authority: Connecticut Attorney General
exemptions: Employment context excluded; governmental, financial, health, and other listed exemptions vary.
penalties: AG guidance: up to $5, 000 per violation under CUTPA; no private CTDPA action.
amendments: PA 25-113 §6 changed applicability effective July 1, 2026; PA 22-15 original Act effective July 1, 2023. PA 26-64 adds separate 2026 changes.

title: Security breach notification
summary: Requires resident and Attorney General notification of covered computerized-data breaches.
scope: Persons owning, licensing, or maintaining covered computerized personal information.
rights: Qualifying SSN or taxpayer-identification-number breaches require 24 months of credit-monitoring services.
obligations: Notify residents and AG; offer applicable monitoring.
deadlines: Residents without unreasonable delay and within 60 days of discovery; AG no later than resident notice.
authority: Connecticut Attorney General
effective: Original PA 05-148 effective 2006-01-01; PA 21-59 60-day revision effective 2021-10-01.
exemptions: Reasonable investigated finding of unlikely individual harm. Timely own-policy and qualifying regulator procedures have conditional compliance routes; HIPAA/HITECH route still requires qualifying AGnotice and SSN/TIN identity-protection services.
penalties: Noncompliance is an unfair trade practice enforced by the Attorney General. CUTPA court remedies include injunctions, restitution and reasonable attorney fees. Under §42-110o, a willful violation permits up to $5,000 per violation; willfulness includes knowing or constructive knowledge of unlawful conduct and violation of an accepted assurance of voluntary compliance. Violating a qualifying restraining order or injunction permits up to $25,000 per violation. These require their respective statutory predicates; neither amount is an automatic fine for every breach.
amendments: PA 23-98 added precise geolocation and other changes.2026 supplementchapter 669 contains no amended §36a-701b; later 2026 session-law reconciliation not certified.

title: 2026 consumer privacy amendments: brokers, facial recognition and genetics
citation: PA 26-64, as amended by PA 26-100 and PA 26-130
summary: Adds broker regulation, facial-recognition safeguards, profiling protections and genetic-testing rights.
scope: Different provisions cover brokers, CTDPA businesses and direct-to-consumer genetic-testing companies.
rights: Genetic customers control samples and results, consent to uses, access/delete data and request sample destruction.
obligations: Security-use facial recognition requires an exclusively maintained matching database and entrance signs linking to its policy. Genetic companies need separate consents and security safeguards.
deadlines: Broker registration: January 1, 2027. Deletion mechanism: July 1, 2028; broker checks every 45 days from October 1, 2028. Pricing requirements postponed to July 1, 2027.
authority: DCP commissioner for broker registration and penalties; AG for CTDPA and genetic-testing enforcement.

penalties: PA 26-100 section 43 permits DCP, following notice and hearing, to impose up to $200 per day per consumer for each violation of broker sections 2–8. Genetic provisions remain AG-only unfair-trade-practice enforcement with no private action under that section.

title: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act
summary: Establishes rights over covered personal data and responsibilities for controllers and processors.
scope: Through 2026: 35, 000 consumers excluding payment-only data, or 10, 000 consumers plus >20% gross revenue from data sales.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt out of covered sales, advertising, and profiling.
obligations: Provide notices, minimize data, protect security, assess high-risk processing, and manage processor duties.
deadlines: Requests: 45 days plus justified 45-day extension; appeals: 60 days. From 2026 cure opportunity is discretionary, not an automatic 60-day entitlement.
authority: Delaware Department of Justice
exemptions: Governmental bodies, financial institutions/affiliates under GLBA, and specified insurance entities excluded; HIPAA and other data exemptions in §12 D-103.
penalties: DOJ-exclusive enforcement as unlawful practice under §2513 and Title 29 consumer-protection powers; no private action. Chapter 12 D sets no standalone dollar amount.
amendments: 85 Del. Laws ch 463 creates versions effective Jan 1, 2027. This summary uses versions effective until then.

title: Computer security breaches
summary: Requires reasonable security and qualifying breach notices.
scope: Delaware businesses owning/licensing computerized resident information; maintainers have owner-notice duties.
rights: Notice and one year of credit monitoring for covered SSN breaches, subject to harm exception.
obligations: Investigate; notify residents; notify AG above 500 affected residents.
deadlines: Resident notice without unreasonable delay, at most 60 days after determination; law-enforcement and late-identification exceptions apply. More than 500 residents: AG by resident notice. Late-identified residents: notify them promptly after identification, and AG within 60 days of breach determination unless timely substitute notice. Owners receive maintainer notice immediately; SSN breaches require one year of monitoring absent unlikely-harm finding.
authority: Delaware Attorney General
effective: Original 2005-06-28; 2017 revision 2018-04-14; 2026 chapter 464/HB 381 signed and effective 2026-09-02.
exemptions: Investigated unlikely-harm determination; qualifying own-policy compliance. Regulator/HIPAA/GLBA notice procedures now satisfy only §12B-102(c) timing, not the whole chapter. Substitute notice includes AG notice.
penalties: AG may seek law/equity relief and direct economic damages under §12 B-104; this chapter specifies no fixed-dollar civil penalty.
amendments: 2026 chapter 464/HB 381 signed and effective September 2, 2026: AG added to substitute notice, AG notice clarified for late-identified residents, and regulator-procedure safe harbor limited to timing. Official bill record and current code corroborate.

title: Delaware Online Privacy and Protection Act
summary: Regulates online privacy notices, children’s marketing, and book-service information.
scope: Covered commercial online services, child-directed operators, and book services.
rights: Privacy transparency and protections for children and reading information.
obligations: Post required privacy disclosures; restrict knowing prohibited marketing using children’s information.
deadlines: Privacy-policy posting violation arises after 30 days notice of noncompliance. Certain non-law-enforcement book disclosures require 35 days to contest; book reporting has March 1 link/disclosure and March 31 report deadlines.
authority: Delaware DOJ Consumer Protection Unit under 6Del.C.§1203C and 29Del.C.§§2520–2526.
exemptions: Child-advertising rules allow specified advertising-service notice and incidental-content exceptions, and impose no age-collection duty. Bookdisclosure/reporting exceptions differ; no blanketprivacy-policy exemption inferred.
penalties: DOJ Consumer Protection enforces through 29Del.C.chapter 25: court civil penalty up to $10,000 per willful violation; administrative penalty up to $5,000 per willful violation. Available remedies include cease-and-desist orders, restitution/disgorgement and state fees/investigation costs. Willful violation of an order/agreement can trigger up to $25,000 per violation. These are separate enforcement routes, not automatic cumulative fines.
amendments: Original 80 Del. Laws ch 148; children’s-marketing provision also cites 80 ch 335 and 84 ch 525.

title: Florida Information Protection Act
summary: Requires data security measures and notice after qualifying security breaches.
scope: Covered entities and third-party agents holding covered personal information.
rights: Qualifying individuals receive notice.
obligations: Take reasonable measures to protect and securely dispose of data; report covered incidents.
deadlines: Resident/Department notice: 30 days after determination/reason to believe; Department threshold 500; agents: 10 days; nationwide reporting agencies above 1, 000. Authorized delays/15-day extension have conditions.

title: Florida Digital Bill of Rights
summary: Provides personal-data rights within a narrowly defined controller framework.
scope: Controller definition: >$1 billion global annual revenue plus≥50% online-ad revenue, covered cloud-connected voice-assistant service, or app platform with≥250, 000 applications; controlled entities included.
rights: Authenticated requests may seek access, correction, deletion and portable copies; opt-outs cover targeted advertising, sale, significant-effect profiling, sensitive data and voice/facial-recognition collection. Inactive device surveillance requires express consumer authorization.
obligations: Determine controller coverage and follow consumer-rights and data-handling provisions.
deadlines: Requests: 45 days plus one justified 15-day extension; compliance notice within 60 days of request. Appeals under §501.707: 60 days.
authority: Florida Department of Legal Affairs
exemptions: State/political subdivisions; GLBA financial institutions/data; HIPAA covered entities/business associates; nonprofits; postsecondary institutions; purely personal/household and specified ad-measurement processing.
penalties: Department-exclusive enforcement; up to $50, 000 per violation, potentially tripled for specified child/deletion/correction/opt-out violations. Discretionary 45-day cure generally excludes child violations.

title: Interception and disclosure of communications
summary: Prohibits specified interception, use, and disclosure of communications, with detailed exceptions.
scope: Persons intercepting or disclosing protected wire, oral, or electronic communications.
rights: Protection against unauthorized interception.
obligations: Establish legally valid consent or a statutory exception before recording/interception.
deadlines: Civil claim within two years after first reasonable opportunity to discover violation; no consumer-request-response clock.

title: Personal identity protection—breach notice
citation: O.C.G.A. §10-1-912; Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 80-3-1-.08 (regulated licensees)
summary: Requires covered information brokers and government data collectors to notify residents about qualifying breaches; service providers must notify the data owner.
scope: Information brokers furnishing personal information to unaffiliated parties for fees/dues; defined state/local government data collectors; and persons/businesses maintaining computerized data for them.
rights: Affected residents receive qualifying notices.
obligations: Provide statutory breach notice; regulated licensees submit a duplicate to their Department.
deadlines: Resident notice as expediently as possible without unreasonable delay; law-enforcement investigation delay allowed. Providers maintaining another covered entity’s data notify it within 24 hours of discovery. More than 10,000 resident notices also trigger nationwide consumer-reporting-agency notice.
authority: Relevant general enforcement authorities; Banking and Finance additionally supervises its regulated licensees. Section 10-1-912 does not designate one exclusive statewide regulator.
effective: 2005-05-05 original Act; 2007-05-24 for Act 241/SB 236 notification amendment.

penalties: Section 10-1-912 states no standalone numeric fine or express civil-damages formula. Other consumer-protection, contract or tort remedies require a separate legal basis; no universal penalty amount is inferred.

title: Student Data Privacy, Accessibility, and Transparency Act
summary: Sets state requirements for student-data privacy and security.
scope: Georgia education agencies and covered education-service operators.
rights: Parents and eligible students may inspect records and request correction. Authorized parents, legal custodians and other eligible recipients receive electronic records under the statutory third-school-business-day deadline; restrictions also govern operators’ advertising, profiling, sale and disclosures.
obligations: Maintain reasonable student-data security. Section 20-2-666(a) restricts targeted advertising, noneducational profiling, sale and disclosure through its explicit-consent and specified-exception structure. Operators must also meet school-requested deletion duties.

title: Standards for Protection of Personal Information
summary: Establishes minimum safeguards for paper and electronic personal information.
scope: Persons owning or licensing Massachusetts residents’ covered personal information.
rights: Information receives required administrative, physical and technical safeguards.
obligations: Maintain a written administrative, technical and physical security program scaled to business size, resources, data volume and consumer/employee confidentiality needs. Designate responsible employees; assess risks, train staff, discipline violations, terminate former-employee access, secure physical records and oversee service providers with contractual safeguards. Monitor safeguards and document incidents and post-incident changes.
exemptions: 201CMR 17 definition ofperson excludes Commonwealth agencies, executive offices, departments, boards, commissions, bureaus, divisions, authorities, branches and political subdivisions. That exclusion does not erase separate public-sector safeguards directed bychapter 93H §2(b)–(c). Small size affects proportional safeguards, not a blanket small-business exemption.
deadlines: Full compliance required by March 1, 2010. Review security measures at least annually and whenever material business-practice changes reasonably affect records security. Historical service-provider contract transition expired March 1, 2012; it is not a current exception.
authority: Massachusetts Attorney General Privacy & Responsible Technology Division enforces ch.93H and 201 CMR 17, alongside ch.93A.
penalties: Chapter 93Hsection 6 authorizes AttorneyGeneral enforcement under Chapter 93Asection 4. That provision permits injunctions, restoration of lost money/property, and up to $5,000 per violation where the person knew or should have known the conduct violated section 2; investigation/litigation costs and fees may also be ordered. Violating a court injunction/order has a separate maximum $10,000 per violation. The regulation does not itself create a standalone automatic per-record fine.
enacted: The original regulation was signed and filed September 19, 2008. The Secretary’s filing form in Massachusetts Register 1114 identifies October 3, 2008 as its publication and effective date. The current revised regulation was signed/filed October 30, 2009 and published/effective November 13, 2009 in Register 1143.
effective: Original regulatory effective date: October 3, 2008; its original compliance deadline was January 1, 2009. The current revision became effective November 13, 2009 and required full compliance by March 1, 2010. Regulatory effect and the deadline for businesses to finish compliance are distinct.
amendments: The original September 19, 2008 filing was published and effective October 3, 2008 (Register 1114, printed pages 71–84). Emergency amendments filed/effective November 14, 2008, published November 28 (Register 1118, pages 34–40), moved general compliance to May 1, 2009 and certain vendor certifications/non-laptop portable-device encryption to January 1, 2010. Amendments filed February 12, 2009 became effective March 6 (Register 1125, pages 49–54): general compliance moved to January 1, 2010, vendor duties changed and wireless-encryption language was clarified. The August 17, 2009 announcement was a proposal followed by a September 22 hearing. Final amendments filed October 30 became effective November 13, 2009 (Register 1143, pages 109–114), adopting the scaled safeguards/vendor framework and March 1, 2010 compliance date. The historical vendor-contract transition ended March 1, 2012; it is not an ongoing exemption.

title: Identity Theft Protection Act: Breach Notice
summary: Requires notice when unauthorized access and acquisition creates qualifying risk to Michigan residents.
scope: Persons and agencies owning, licensing or maintaining databases containing covered information.
rights: Residents receive notice describing the incident, information type, assistance contact, and vigilance steps.
obligations: Notify owners for maintained data; notify national credit bureaus when more than 1,000 residents are notified, subject to exceptions.
exemptions: No notice if prudent investigation finds no likely substantial loss, injury or identity theft; HIPAA and financial-institution compliance provisions apply.
deadlines: Without unreasonable delay; scope/restoration and law-enforcement delays permitted.
authority: Michigan AG or prosecuting attorney.
penalties: Knowing notice failure: up to $250 each failed notice, aggregate $750,000 for same breach; AG/prosecutor action. Fraudulent false-breach notice separately misdemeanor with graduated $250/$500/$750 fines and up to 93 days; other civil remedies preserved.
effective: Original added section effective July 2, 2007; 2010 amendment effective April 1, 2011. Distinct §445.72(16) application text covers discovery/notification occurring on/after July 2, 2006.
amendments: Current official history lists 2006 Act 566 and 2010 Act 315; do not collapse statutory application date July 2, 2006 into original effective date July 2, 2007.

title: Internet Privacy Protection Act
summary: Restricts employer and educational-institution demands for access to personal internet accounts.
scope: Employers, educational institutions, employees, applicants, students and prospective students.
rights: Protection against prohibited access demands and retaliation.
obligations: Do not require disclosure of protected account-access information except within statutory exceptions.
exemptions: Employer-paid devices, business accounts, specific misconduct/proprietary-data investigations, lawful network monitoring and legally mandated screening preserved; educational institution supplied devices/accounts and public information excepted; compliance-with-law affirmative defense.
deadlines: Written demand with reasonable violation documentation at least 60 days before damages action or adding damages claim; not a general 60-day claim-filing limit.
authority: Courts through civil and criminal provisions.
penalties: Violation of §§37.273 or .274: misdemeanor fine up to $1,000; private injunction and damages up to $1,000 plus reasonable attorney fees/costs.
amendments: Official PDF rendered October 22, 2026, complete through PA 114 of 2026; all section histories still list 2012 Act 478 without subsequent amendments.

title: Data Warehouses: Security Breach Notice
summary: Requires residents to be notified of qualifying unauthorized acquisition of personal information.
scope: Persons/businesses conducting business in Minnesota and owning or licensing covered data.
rights: Affected residents receive notice; statutory waiver is void.
obligations: Maintainers notify owners immediately; coordinate national credit bureau notices when over 500 persons are notified.
exemptions: Financial institutions defined by 15USC 6809(3) excluded; good-faith employee acquisition without further use/disclosure not a breach; qualifying own notification procedures satisfy notice duties.
deadlines: Residents: most expedient time possible without unreasonable delay; credit bureaus: within 48 hours when the statutory threshold is met. Law-enforcement delay allowed.
authority: Minnesota Attorney General under §8.31.
penalties: AG enforcement under §8.31 includes injunction and court civil penalty up to $25,000 under subdivision 3; do not confuse this general enforcement amount with MCDPA’s specific $7,500 schedule.
enacted: June 2, 2005; Chapter 167, approved by the Governor and filed June 3.
effective: January 1, 2006, as recorded in official final legislative actions.
amendments: Official current section history: 2005 c 167 §1; 2006 c 212 art 1 §§17,24; 2006 c 233 §§7,8. Government-data provision formerly subdivision 5 renumbered §13.055 subd 6.

title: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act
summary: Provides Minnesota consumer data rights and business privacy safeguards.
scope: Minnesota business/targeting entities processing at least 100,000 consumers annually, excluding payment-only data; alternatively 25,000 consumers and over 25% gross revenue from personal-data sales. School technology providers also comply with §13.32, which prevails in conflicts.
rights: Confirm/access categories, correct, delete, obtain portable provided data, identify specific recipient third parties and opt out of sale, targeting or significant profiling. Question profiling results, obtain reasons and feasible alternatives, review input data and seek correction/reevaluation. Authorized agents, guardians and qualifying opt-out signals supported.
obligations: Accessible multilingual privacy notice, clear opt-out route, material-change notification, data minimization/inventory and security. Obtain sensitive-data consent and parental consent for known children; known 13–16 targeting/sales need consent. Cease consent-based processing within 15 days of revocation. Prevent unlawful discrimination, unnecessary retention and contractual waiver of consumer rights.
exemptions: Government/tribal entities and specified health, research, public-health, FCRA, GLBA, DPPA, FERPA, FarmCredit and employment-context data excluded under conditions. Financial/health data exclusions are not automatic immunity for every entity operation. Specific small-business rules and deferred postsecondary compliance must be applied separately.
deadlines: Opt-out compliance as soon as feasible, no later than 45 days. Other responses 45 days with one necessary 45-day extension; timely reasons required. Appeals 45 days, extendable 60 days with notice. Appeal records retained 24 months; information free twice annually. Sensitive identifiers are described rather than disclosed in full.
authority: Minnesota Attorney General enforces through civil proceedings.
penalties: Injunction and civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation; state litigation expenses may be recovered. No private right, including through §8.31 subdivision 3a. Mandatory 30-day warning/cure paragraph expired January 31, 2026 and must not be shown as currently guaranteed.
effective: 2025-07-31; covered postsecondary institutions regulated by Office of Higher Education not required to comply until 2029-07-31.
amendments: Current 2026 text retains expired 2026 cure paragraph as historical text. OHE-regulated postsecondary institutions’ compliance deferral runs through July 31, 2029 under 2024 chapter 121 article 5 §14.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Internet Service Provider Privacy
summary: Protects paid household internet subscribers against unauthorized disclosure of identifiable service information.
scope: Internet providers serving consumers in Minnesota who pay for personal/family/household access and do not resell access.
rights: Obtain own identifiable information by written/electronic request at no more than retrieval cost; authorize disclosure with described recipients/uses.
obligations: Do not knowingly disclose beyond statutory permissions; take reasonable security/privacy steps. Authorization must follow conspicuous contract terms, including any disclosed opt-out model.
exemptions: Required lawful subpoenas, warrants, orders and authorized investigations; necessary provider debt litigation; ordinary-course business, provider acceptable-use enforcement and consumer authorization. Reasonable implemented prevention practices are a civil defense. Unapproved/unparticipated criminal hacking is excluded from provider security liability.
deadlines: No numeric access-response clock in §325M.03. Federal-preemption-triggered expiration is conditional, not a calendar sunset.
authority: Consumers may sue under §325M.07.
penalties: Prevailing/substantially prevailing consumer receives greater of $500 or actual damages; costs and reasonable fees may be awarded. Class actions prohibited. Unlawfully obtained information generally excluded from civil evidence except to prove this law’s violation.
amendments: Original 2002 history remains in reviewed sections; current 2026 compilation separately adds broader consumer/social-media laws without conflating them with these ISP provisions.

title: Insurance Data Security Law
summary: Creates risk-based information security and cybersecurity-event investigation/reporting duties for insurance licensees.
scope: Licensees regulated by the Mississippi Insurance Commissioner.
rights: Protects nonpublic information; this is sector-specific rather than comprehensive consumer privacy.
obligations: Maintain written security program, investigate events and oversee third-party providers; domestic insurers certify compliance annually.
exemptions: Partial exemptions include fewer than 50 employees, revenue below $5 million, assets below $10 million, and producers/adjusters; HIPAA and qualifying affiliate programs have compliance provisions.
deadlines: Qualifying events: Commissioner notice within three business days of determination; annual domestic insurer certification begins February 15, 2021.
authority: Mississippi Insurance Commissioner.
penalties: Commissioner may impose penalties under Miss.Code §83-5-85 and remedy security deficiencies; §83-5-819 cross-refers to that general insurance penalty provision rather than setting its own numeric amount.
amendments: SB 2831 signed April 3, 2019; MID Bulletin 2019-4 confirms July 1, 2019 effective date, one-year security-program and two-year vendor phase-ins. No later amendment conclusion made.

title: State Enterprise Security Program: Incident Reporting
summary: Requires state-agency cybersecurity incident reporting under the enterprise security framework.
scope: State agencies, employees, trusted partners and authorized users of state assets; covers paper/electronic information and resources hosted by third parties. Agencies outside the EnterpriseStateNetwork must maintain appropriate policies consistent with the policy’s intent.
rights: Protects state-held information through incident handling and security oversight.
obligations: Agency heads remain accountable for agency-wide security, designated information-security officers, written policies, safeguards, internal assessments and procurement security requirements, including third-party-hosted resources. Policy controls cover information regardless of medium or location. Agencies must review compliance, document deficiencies and plan remediation.
exemptions: Some technical controls apply only to EnterpriseStateNetwork participants; nonparticipants must instead maintain environment-appropriate policies consistent with the enterprise policy’s intent. Agency policies must use the more restrictive rule in conflicts; this does not exempt nonparticipants from all security obligations.
deadlines: Report to ITS no later than close of next business day following discovery. Applies to agency/contractor/other-managed information systems; participation in Enterprise State Network also brings an entity within reporting scope.
authority: Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services; state enterprise security oversight.
penalties: Rule 1.11 provides audit findings and State Auditor directions for corrective action, documentation of noncompliance and corrective plans. The rule creates no independent numeric fine or private damages schedule. Separate laws apply on their own terms; this policy does not grant immunity.
enacted: March 10, 2017; HB 999 approved by GovernorBryant, establishing section 25-53-201.
effective: July 1, 2017 for the original EnterpriseSecurityProgram, expressly confirmed by ITS’s 2017 LegislativeSummary. Later 2025 HB 958 changes commenced July 1, 2025 as separately sourced.
amendments: ITS confirms 2025 HB 958 amended §25-53-201 and related authority: approved April 17, 2025, effective July 1, 2025. This identifies an actual later amendment, not the original program commencement.

title: Security Breach Notification
summary: Requires consumer notification following qualifying unauthorized access and acquisition of personal information.
scope: Owners/licensees of Missouri residents’ personal information and Missouri businesses holding it.
rights: Affected consumers receive notice subject to statutory findings and exceptions.
obligations: Maintainers notify owners immediately; investigate and issue prescribed notifications.
exemptions: No notice if appropriate investigation/agency consultation finds identity theft/fraud not reasonably likely; document for five years. Qualifying regulator-compliant programs and GLBA/financial interagency guidance compliance provisions apply.
deadlines: Residents without unreasonable delay; maintainers notify owners immediately; over 1,000 consumers at once triggers AG/national credit bureau notice without unreasonable delay.
authority: Missouri Attorney General has exclusive authority under §407.1500(4) to sue for actual damages for willful and knowing violations and may seek the statutory civil penalty.
penalties: For willful and knowing violations, AG may obtain actual damages and seek up to $150,000 per breach or series of similar breaches discovered in one investigation. The cap is not a per-person assessment; this section assigns the action exclusively to AG.
amendments: Current official section lists 2009 HB 62 and August 28, 2009 effective date, with no later statutory amendment in its history.

title: Library Records Confidentiality
summary: Protects patron privacy in library records, including records held by contractors.
scope: Libraries, library staff and contracted third parties receiving or storing library records.
rights: Patrons may complain to the AG and bring a civil claim for compromised privacy.
obligations: Do not disclose library records except authorized disclosures.
exemptions: Patron written request or qualifying court order for public safety/crime prosecution.
deadlines: Written AG complaint within 180 days of alleged violation; separate private circuit-court damages action authorized without an express filing period in this section.
authority: Missouri Attorney General and circuit courts.
penalties: Private damages, discretionary punitive damages, equitable relief and prevailing-party attorney fees. Respondent fees only when case without foundation. AG may initiate legal action after reviewing complaint; no fixed numeric fine stated.
effective: Original version effective 1986-08-13; current amended version effective 2014-08-28.
amendments: 1986 HB 1372 §2; 2014 HB 1085 amendment. Official version table shows 1986-to 2014 predecessor and current 2014 version.

title: Computer Security Breach
summary: Requires notice for unauthorized acquisition materially compromising personal data and causing or reasonably believed to cause loss/injury.
scope: Montana businesses owning/licensing computerized personal information.
rights: Affected residents receive statutory notice.
obligations: Maintainers notify owners immediately; simultaneously send notice copy, distribution details and affected count to AG consumer protection office.
exemptions: Good-faith employee acquisition without further unauthorized use/disclosure excluded; law-enforcement delay allowed.
deadlines: Without unreasonable delay; AG submission simultaneous with individual notice.
authority: Montana Attorney General consumer protection office.
penalties: Via §30-14-1705 and §30-14-142: civil fine up to $10,000 each for willful unlawful practices and up to $10,000 each injunction/TRO violation; fraudulent-course conviction up to $5,000 and/or 1 year. Willfulness means knew or should have known.

title: Financial Data Protection and Consumer Notification
summary: Requires breach investigation and notice when unauthorized use occurred or is reasonably likely.
scope: Nebraska businesses owning/licensing computerized personal information of residents.
rights: Residents receive qualifying notice; statutory waivers are void.
obligations: Investigate reasonably and promptly; notify affected residents and AG under the Act.
exemptions: Regulator-compliant notice procedures may satisfy the statute.
deadlines: As soon as possible and without unreasonable delay, subject to law-enforcement and system-restoration needs.
authority: Nebraska Attorney General.
penalties: AG may subpoena and recover direct economic damages for each injured Nebraska resident under §87-803. Security §87-808 violation invokes ConsumerProtection Act enforcement and creates no private cause under that security provision.
enacted: 2006 LB 876 established Act; §87-806 source amended 2018 LB 757 §8.
effective: Applies to discovery of or notification pertaining to system breaches occurring on or after July 14, 2006, expressly stated in section 87-807(LB 876 section 7). This is the statute’s operational applicability date.
amendments: Current §87-806 separates breach-notice recovery from §87-808 security ConsumerProtection Act route; do not apply no-private-action language indiscriminately to unrelated claims.

title: Nebraska Data Privacy Act
summary: Creates consumer rights and processing duties, with a small-business framework rather than general numerical consumer thresholds.
scope: Businesses serving Nebraska residents and processing/selling personal data, generally excluding federally defined small businesses.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out rights under §§87-1107–87-1111.
obligations: Data minimization, reasonable security, privacy notices and appeals.
exemptions: Government, specified financial/health entities, nonprofits, higher education and specified utilities excluded; small businesses retain sensitive-data sale consent obligations.
deadlines: Respond without undue delay within 45 days; one reasonably necessary 45-day extension requires notice and reasons within the original period. Denial with justification and appeal instructions within 45 days. Information free up to twice annually; manifestly unfounded, excessive or repetitive requests may incur reasonable administrative fees or refusal. Separately the existing 60-day appeal determination is governed by §87-1109.
authority: Nebraska Attorney General exclusively.
penalties: After statutory cure period or breach of written cure statement: civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation; AG injunction and reasonable investigation/litigation expenses and fees.
amendments: 2024 LB 1074 established the Act; official AG guidance confirms January 1, 2025 commencement.

title: Age Verification: Identification Retention Ban
summary: Combines adult-content age verification with a ban on retaining identification afterward.
scope: Commercial websites knowingly/intentionally publishing harmful-to-minors material comprising more than one-third of total content; age-verification entities also face retention limits.
rights: An individual harmed by prohibited identification retention may sue; minors/parents/guardians have qualifying access-verification claims.
obligations: Use reasonable age verification and retain no identifying information after granting access.
exemptions: News-gathering and bona fide news/public-interest material exempt. Mere connectivity/transmission/storage does not make an Internet utility liable for content it does not create/control.
deadlines: Identification nonretention begins once access is granted; no general request-response clock.
authority: Courts through aggrieved-person civil actions.
penalties: Actual damages caused by qualifying verification/retention violations; appropriate preliminary/equitable/declaratory relief and discretionary reasonable fees/litigation costs. No fixed dollar award in §87-1004.
effective: July 19, 2024, expressly reproduced in the section’s effective-date note by Justia’s 2024 Nebraska Code mirror.
amendments: Current source notes list 2024 LB 1092; current litigation/injunction status not independently resolved.

title: Personal Information Security and Breach Notification
summary: Combines reasonable security, disposal, encryption/payment-card standards and breach notification.
scope: Covered data collectors handling Nevada residents’ personal information.
rights: Residents receive notice of covered security breaches.
obligations: Maintain safeguards; comply with applicable encryption and payment-card requirements; notify on qualifying breaches.
exemptions: §603A.220(5): qualifying own timing-consistent notice procedures and GLBA privacy/security compliance deemed notice compliant. §220(7) excludes Chapter 675 licensees from this notice section. Do not apply that exception automatically to all separate security duties.
deadlines: Residents most expedient possible without unreasonable delay; owners immediately after maintainer discovery. Law-enforcement delay ends when investigation not compromised. Over 1,000 at once: nationwide bureau notice without unreasonable delay.
authority: Nevada Attorney General; precise remedies depend on provision.
penalties: §603A.260 invokes deceptive-practice enforcement; §290 AG/district-attorney injunction. §§270–280 permit notifying collector damages/appropriate punitive damages, fees/costs against unlawful acquirer/beneficiary, and court-ordered notification-cost restitution after conviction. These are distinct from consumer private remedies.
enacted: June 17, 2005; Chapter 485, SB 347, approved by the Governor. Sections 14–28 established the data-collector framework.
effective: January 1, 2006 for original data-collector provisions in sections 14–28, expressly assigned by section 30(2). October 1, 2005 applied to different sections of the same act and must not be used as the breach provision’s original date.
amendments: 2021 Chapter 256/AB 61 section 19, approved June 2, 2021, adds the 603A.260 deceptive-trade-practice consequence; no special commencement clause appears, so 218D.330 supplies October 1, 2021. 2023 Chapter 527/SB 355 section 17, approved June 15, 2023, exempts Chapter 675 licensed lenders from 603A.220; section 27 expressly makes this operative October 1, 2023, with preparatory administration upon approval. Those lenders have separate breach duties under the same act. 2017 Chapter 570/SB 538, approved June 12, 2017, establishes online-privacy provisions and makes conforming security-subchapter references; absent a special date, October 1, 2017 applies.

title: Online Privacy Notices and Sale Opt-Out
summary: Regulates covered online operators and data brokers, including privacy notices and sale opt-outs; not a general all-sector privacy act.
scope: Commercial online operators with the specified Nevada nexus, and businesses primarily buying and selling covered information about Nevada consumers with whom they lack a direct relationship. Covered information is the listed identifiers or other information combined with an identifier.
rights: Verified opt-out of defined sale of covered information.
obligations: Provide required notice and designated request address; honor qualifying sale opt-outs.
exemptions: Operator exclusions include service providers acting for an owner, HIPAA-covered entities, specified vehicle-service data and persons not collecting, maintaining or selling covered information. Section 603A.338 separately excludes consumer-reporting agencies, specified FCRA/GLBA/DPPA-regulated information, fraud-prevention activities, public information and separately regulated consumer-health data. The narrow Nevada small-operator exception concerns notice, not a blanket exemption from every duty.
deadlines: Operators and data brokers: respond to verified sale opt-out requests within 60 days, extendable up to 30 days with notice if reasonably necessary. First failures may qualify for 30-day cure under §§603A.347–.349.
authority: Nevada Attorney General.
penalties: Attorney General injunction or civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation under §603A.360; no private action against an operator created by these provisions; other remedies preserved.
enacted: Original online-notice law: SB 538, Chapter 570, approved June 12, 2017. SB 220, Chapter 211, approved May 29, 2019 added sale opt-outs. SB 260, Chapter 292, approved June 2, 2021 added data-broker requirements.
effective: Original notice law: October 1, 2017. The 2019 opt-out amendment: October 1, 2019. Neither act specifies another date, so these dates follow NRS 218D.330. The official SB 260 docket expressly gives October 1, 2021 for the data-broker amendments.
amendments: 2019 SB 220 added sale opt-outs and revised operator exclusions. 2021 SB 260 expanded sale coverage and data-broker duties, established first-failure cure provisions and revised exemptions. Current 603A.338 history also records a 2023 amendment excluding separately regulated consumer-health data.

title: Expectation of Privacy
summary: Gives New Hampshire residents personal-data rights and regulates covered businesses.
scope: State business/targeting and 35,000 unique consumers per one-year period excluding payment-only data; alternatively 10,000 consumers and over 25% gross revenue from personal-data sales.
rights: Confirm/access, correct, delete, portable automated-data copy and opt out of sale, targeted advertising and significant solely automated profiling; use agents/guardians and appeal refusals. Trade secrets protected; opt-outs need no authentication absent documented reasonable fraud concern.
obligations: Limit collection/purposes; maintain security, clear accessible notice and opt-out method. Sensitive processing needs consent and known-child processing followsCOPPA. Stop consent-based processing within 15 days of revocation. Known 13–15 targeting/sale needs consent; do not discriminate for exercising rights.
exemptions: Government, nonprofits, higher education, registered national securities associations, GLBA institutions/data and HIPAA covered entities/business associates excluded. Separate conditional exclusions cover health/research/patient-safety/public-health, FCRA, DPPA, FERPA, FarmCredit, role-based employment/contact/benefit and preempted airline data. Personal/household processing and necessary legal/security uses have further limitations.
deadlines: Requests 45 days with one reasonably necessary 45-day extension and timely notice. Refusals within 45 days; written appeals within 60 days. One free response per 12 months; excessive/unfounded/repetitive requests may face reasonable cost or refusal.
authority: Attorney General has exclusive enforcement under §507-H: 11.
penalties: AG consumer-protection injunction/restitution and incorporated §358-A: 4 civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation; no private right under this chapter. Since January 1, 2026 an opportunity to cure is discretionary; if notice is granted, cure within 60 days. Mandatory 2025 treatment has expired.
enacted: March 6, 2024; SB 255 signed by the Governor as Chapter 5.
effective: January 1, 2025, as recorded in the official bill docket.
amendments: Current §6 includes a new child-data sale prohibition effective January 1, 2027. It is prospective as of November 10, 2026; current teen/child consent protections already apply.

title: Right to Privacy: Security Breach Notice
summary: Requires investigation and qualifying notification for compromised computerized personal information.
scope: Persons including businesses and governmental entities, as defined in §359-C: 19.
rights: Affected residents receive qualifying notices.
obligations: Determine likelihood of misuse and notify affected residents and the appropriate regulator/AG as applicable.
exemptions: Public government-record data and good-faith business employee acquisition without further use/disclosure excluded. Regulated trade/commerce notification-program compliance qualifies under §20(V). GLBA TitleV exemption in §20(VI)(b) is from additional bureau notice, not a blanket exemption from every duty.
deadlines: Prompt misuse determination; if misuse occurred, likely or undetermined, affected notice as soon/quickly as possible. Maintainer-to-owner immediately. Over 1,000 consumers: national bureau notice without unreasonable delay; regulatory or AG notice also required.
authority: New Hampshire Attorney General or applicable industry regulator.
penalties: An injured person may recover actual damages and equitable relief. Knowing or willful violation requires double to triple actual damages; prevailing plaintiffs receive costs and reasonable attorney fees. Attempted damage-right waivers are unenforceable. Private injunctions may be available without bond at court discretion. AG enforcement proceeds under RSA 358-A: 4; the responsible person bears the burden of demonstrating compliance.
effective: January 1, 2007, as expressly stated in the source notes to RSA 359-C: 19–21.
amendments: Official breach-subdivision source notes cite 2006 chapter 242 §1 effective January 1, 2007. These notes do not identify subsequent amendments to §§19–21.

title: New Jersey Data Privacy Act
summary: Establishes comprehensive personal-data protections and consumer rights.
scope: Controllers serving/targeting New Jersey residents: at least 100,000 consumers excluding payment-only data, or at least 25,000 consumers plus revenue/discount from personal-data sales.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-outs concerning sale, targeting and profiling.
obligations: Disclose processing categories, purposes, recipients and contact methods; explain opt-outs for sales, targeting and significant profiling. Do not require creation of a new account to exercise rights. Authenticate relevant requests with commercially reasonable efforts; opt-outs need no authentication, although documented reasonable fraud suspicion permits denial with explanation.
exemptions: Consumers act in individual/household rather than commercial/employment contexts.
deadlines: Verified requests: 45 days; reasonably necessary 45-day extension with reasons notified within the original period. Refusal justification and appeal instructions within 45 days. Written appeal decision within 45 days of receipt; denied appeal must include a route to the Division. One free response per 12 months. Prior-collected data remain covered if processing continues after commencement.
authority: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs/Attorney General.

title: Security Breach Notification Act
summary: Requires notice when covered computerized personal information is accessed and acquired without authorization and the statutory fraud or identity-theft condition is met.
enacted: 2008, chapter 86; amended by 2025, chapter 406 (SB 626), filed June 2, 2025 without Governor signature.
effective: Original notice section November 1, 2008; 2025 amendments January 1, 2026.
authority: Attorney General or district attorney has exclusive enforcement authority, except state-chartered/licensed financial institutions are enforced exclusively by their primary state regulator (§ 165).
scope: Individuals and entities owning or licensing computerized personal information of Oklahoma residents.
rights: Qualifying affected residents receive breach notification.
obligations: Determine whether the statutory notice trigger is met and notify covered residents.
exemptions: Encryption/redaction does not avoid notice if readable information or its keys were acquired and identity theft/fraud is reasonably expected. Public information is excluded. Consistent internal notice procedures satisfy resident-notice duties. Qualifying federal, HIPAA or Oklahoma hospital notification compliance also satisfies resident notice only if required AG notice is provided (§ 164).
penalties: Actual damages and up to $150,000 per breach or similar series investigated together. Reasonable safeguards plus required notice protect against civil penalties. deadlines: Resident notice without unreasonable delay, subject to investigation, system restoration and authorized law-enforcement delay. Maintainers notify the owner as soon as practicable after determination. AG notice without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after resident notice; fewer than 500 affected residents are exempt from AG notice, or fewer than 1,000 for a credit-reporting agency breach.
amendments: 2008 chapter 86 originally effective November 1, 2008. 2025 chapter 406 amendments effective January 1, 2026; § 166 applies the revised act to breach determination/notification occurring from that date.

Section 5.4 requires specified credit-report access and 12 months of no-cost credit monitoring when covered names and SSNs, bank-account or government-ID numbers were accessed. deadlines: Notify residents within 60 days of discovery/notification. After law-enforcement delay ends, notify within 30 days of the agency’s determination. Notify AG for more than 250 residents; a no-likely-harm determination still requires AG notice and three-year written documentation. Nationwide credit agencies must be notified without unreasonable delay.

title: Tennessee Information Protection Act
summary: Provides consumer control over personal information and obligations for covered controllers and processors.
effective: July 1, 2025. Assessment duties apply to processing activities created or generated on or after July 1, 2024, as confirmed by AG guidance.
authority: Tennessee Attorney General Division of Consumer Affairs.
scope: Over $25 million annual revenue plus 175,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers and at least 50% gross revenue from data sales, under the AG guide.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, and qualifying opt-outs for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling.
obligations: Privacy notices, rights procedures, appeals, and data protection requirements.
exemptions: Includes government, financial institutions, HIPAA-covered entities/business associates, nonprofits, and higher education.
penalties: AG exclusive enforcement: civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation, declaratory/injunctive relief, reasonable attorney fees and investigative costs. Court may award treble damages for willful or knowing violations. No private or class action based on a violation.
deadlines: Consumer request response 45 days, subject to statutory extension conditions; appeal decision 60 days. AG must provide 60 days’ written notice and opportunity to cure. A cure and express written assurance prevent the noticed action unless violation persists or recurs.
amendments: 2023 Public Chapter 408 enacted TIPA. Adopted HA 0348 replaced introduced text. Official 2025 code reenactment compilation places the law in part 33 (§§ 47-18-3301–3315), resolving proposed part-32 numbering; subsequent 2025–2026 amendments have not been exhaustively excluded.

title: State Agency Computerized Data Breach Reporting
summary: Requires state agencies to report suspected or confirmed unauthorized acquisition of computerized data and suspected or confirmed breaches of the systems that protect it to the Comptroller.
enacted: 2015 Public Chapter 42 (SB 416) added governmental computer-breach reporting to § 8-4-119; governor signed March 27, 2015. The broader fraud-report section originated in 2012 chapter 946.
effective: March 27, 2015 for the breach-reporting amendment, confirmed by official SB 416 history.
authority: Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury.
scope: Each state board, commission, committee, department, office or other state-government unit. Covered systems include those operated/administered by the agency or a contractor; the duty is not limited to personal information. This particular reporting channel does not cover private organizations.
rights: Agency accountability and oversight; this section is not a general consumer access-rights law.
obligations: Notify the Comptroller of covered suspected or confirmed events.
exemptions: Individual malware/spyware occurrences are excluded under §8-4-119(c)(2)(A); Comptroller guidance requires reporting when an occurrence causes unauthorized computerized-data acquisition or compromises the protective security system. The duty is not restricted to acquisition of personal information.
penalties: Section 8-4-119 creates reporting and confidentiality duties, without a separate monetary fine, damages formula or private action in that section. Comptroller review is oversight, not an automatic compensation award.
deadlines: Report within a reasonable time under the circumstances, with an absolute maximum of five working days after confirmation or suspicion. Waiting five days is not automatically reasonable in every case. Reports are confidential Comptroller working papers.
amendments: Code mirror history lists 2012 chapter 946 and 2015 chapter 42; official current Comptroller guidance confirms the five-working-day computer-breach duty. No later amendment is shown in the reviewed mirror.

title: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
summary: Creates consumer data rights, security duties, processor responsibilities, and assessments for higher-risk processing.
authority: Texas Attorney General; exclusive enforcement and no private right of action.
scope: Texas-facing persons processing or selling personal data who are not SBA-defined small businesses; § 541.107 separately requires small businesses to obtain prior consumer consent for sensitive-data sales.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, and qualifying opt-outs.
obligations: Provide privacy notices, rights and appeal procedures, reasonable security, and required assessments.
exemptions: Government, GLBA financial institutions/data, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, nonprofits, higher education, and specified electricity entities. Section 541.003 separately excludes health records and enumerated regulated information.
penalties: Up to $7,500 per violation after the cure process or breach of a cure statement.
deadlines: Consumer requests: respond without undue delay and within 45 days; one additional 45-day extension with explanation during the initial period. Denials must explain appeal rights within 45 days. Appeal decision within 60 days. Attorney General must give 30 days to cure before enforcement.

title: Identity Theft Enforcement and Protection Act — Breach Notice
summary: Requires affected-consumer notices and electronic reports to the Attorney General for breaches reaching the Texas-resident threshold.
effective: Codification effective April 1, 2009; electronic AG reporting change effective September 1, 2023.
authority: Texas Attorney General.
scope: Businesses and organizations experiencing covered system-security breaches.
rights: Affected consumers receive breach notice under the statute.
obligations: Report qualifying breaches electronically using the OAG reporting form and give consumer notices.
exemptions: Sensitive-information definitions and exceptions require statutory review.
penalties: Section 521.151: $2,000–$50,000 civil penalty per chapter violation. Failure to take reasonable action to provide resident notice additionally permits up to $100 per affected individual per consecutive day, capped at $250,000 for one breach. AG may seek injunction and equitable relief.
deadlines: Consumer notice without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the person determines the breach occurred, subject to statutory investigation, restoration and law-enforcement delay provisions. A maintainer must notify the owner/licensee immediately after discovering a qualifying breach. For at least 250 Texas residents, report electronically to the Attorney General as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after determining the breach occurred. Notice to more than 10,000 persons at one time also requires nationwide consumer reporting agency notice without unreasonable delay.
amendments: Current § 521.053 and current AG guidance checked; full chronology remains open.

title: Utah Consumer Privacy Act
summary: Establishes rights relating to personal data, controller and processor requirements, and public enforcement.
effective: Original Act effective December 31, 2023; motor-vehicle Part 5 is effective January 1, 2027.
authority: Utah Division of Consumer Protection and Attorney General.
scope: Controllers/processors doing business in Utah or targeting Utah residents, with annual revenue of at least $25 million, and either processing at least 100,000 consumers yearly or processing at least 25,000 while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from personal-data sales. Statutory entity/data exclusions also apply.
rights: Confirm processing, access, delete consumer-provided data, portability of consumer-provided data, correct inaccuracies, and opt out of sale and targeted advertising. Correction was added by 2025 chapter 468.
obligations: Provide prescribed consumer rights processes and controller/processor protections.
exemptions: Section 13-61-102 excludes governmental entities and processors acting on their behalf, tribes, institutions of higher education, nonprofits, HIPAA covered entities and business associates. Enumerated data exemptions include HIPAA and specified health/research information, regulated FCRA activities, GLBA institutions/affiliates and regulated data, DPPA, FERPA and Farm Credit data, employment/applicant/contractor-role data and specified emergency-contact/benefit information. Personal or household processing and specified air-carrier activity are excluded. The chapter contains a separate future January 1, 2027 version; those future provisions are not represented as operative in 2026.
penalties: AG may recover actual consumer damages and up to $7,500 for each violation after failure to cure or renewed violation. Qualifying cure plus written assurance prevents the noticed enforcement action.
deadlines: 45-day request response, one reasonably necessary 45-day extension with explanation before initial period expires. AG gives 30 days’ notice and cure opportunity.
amendments: 2025 chapter 468 added correction. Current PDF also contains 2026 amendments and separately labeled January 1, 2027 motor-vehicle provisions; future motor-vehicle text is not treated as currently operative.

2.notes: Comprehensive-law biometric sensitive-data notice/opt-out requirements, not standalone biometric collection law.

title: Protection of Personal Information Act
summary: Requires prompt investigation of qualifying security breaches and notice where misuse for identity theft or fraud has occurred or is reasonably likely.
enacted: 2006 SB 69, Laws of Utah chapter 343, signed March 20, 2006. The original chapter was titled Consumer Credit Protection Act; 2009 HB 234 renamed it Protection of Personal Information Act.
effective: January 1, 2007 under § 7 of original enrolled SB 69. Later amendments have separate effective dates.
authority: Utah Attorney General; Utah Cyber Center receives qualifying notifications.
scope: Owners or licensees of computerized personal information concerning Utah residents; financial institution exclusion in § 13-44-103.
rights: Affected residents receive qualifying notice.
obligations: Conduct good-faith investigation; send resident and applicable regulator/credit-agency notices.
exemptions: Chapter excludes financial institutions and their GLBA-defined affiliates. Good-faith employee acquisition is excluded unless unlawfully used or improperly disclosed; public-record/public-media information is outside personal-information definition.
penalties: AG enforcement; no private action is created, while existing contract/tort rights are preserved. Up to $2,500 per consumer violation/series and generally $100,000 aggregate for related violations; aggregate cap exceptions include 10,000 Utah plus 10,000 out-of-state consumers, or greater settlement. Injunctions, fees and costs available.
deadlines: Prompt reasonable investigation; notice in the most expedient time without unreasonable delay after scope and system integrity determined, subject to law-enforcement delay. Maintainers notify owners immediately when misuse occurs or is likely. AG and Utah Cyber Center notice for 500 or more Utah residents; nationwide credit agencies for 1,000 or more. Administrative enforcement must start within ten years after the alleged breach last occurred; civil enforcement within five years (§ 13-44-301(12)).
amendments: Original 2006 chapter 343 was signed March 20, 2006 and commenced January 1, 2007. Later chapter history identifies 2009 chapter 61 renaming, 2019 chapter 348 financial-institution exclusions, 2024 chapter 426 reporting changes, and 2025 chapter 173 enforcement amendments.

title: Data Broker Registration and Security Duties
summary: Requires qualifying data brokers to register annually and maintain written safeguards for personal information.
effective: Original registration provision effective January 1, 2019. Act 138 changes described below take effect January 1, 2027; they are future requirements as of November 10, 2026.
authority: Secretary of State administers registration; Attorney General may sue in Superior Court’s Civil Division for current registration penalties and injunctions.
scope: Businesses knowingly collecting and selling or licensing brokered personal information of consumers without a direct relationship.
rights: Public registration transparency; this is not asserted to create a universal deletion right.
obligations: Through 2026, annual registration costs $100 and includes contact, opt-out, credentialing, breach and minor-data disclosures. From January 1, 2027, § 2446 requires $900 registration, a $20,000 bond, broader disclosures and a consumer-rights webpage link.
exemptions: Direct-relationship, incidental-sale, directory, professional-information, and specified alert-service exclusions.
penalties: Through 2026, nonregistration costs $50 daily, capped at $10,000 yearly, plus unpaid fees and other lawful penalties. From January 1, 2027: $200 daily nonregistration; omitted information uncorrected after 30 days costs $1,000 daily; materially incorrect information costs $25,000 plus $1,000 daily if not corrected within 30 days.
deadlines: Through 2026, register by January 31 after a qualifying year. From January 1, 2027, initial registration within 30 days of becoming a broker, then annually by July 1. A bond action must be brought within two years after accrual.
amendments: Original 2017 Act 171 (Adjourned Session), § 2, effective January 1, 2019. 2025 Act 138 (Adjourned Session), § 1, changes § 2446 effective January 1, 2027.
