title: Security Breach Notice Act
summary: Requires consumer and regulator notice after covered breaches of personally identifiable information or login credentials.
effective: Original effective January 1, 2007. Separately labeled future amendments take effect January 1, 2027.
authority: Vermont Attorney General or Department of Financial Regulation, as applicable.
scope: Data collectors owning, licensing, or maintaining covered information.
rights: Consumer breach notice and special safeguards for compromised login credentials.
obligations: Notify residents and regulators; maintainers notify data owners immediately.
exemptions: Documented no-misuse-possible findings and limited regulated-entity compliance exceptions apply.
penalties: AG and State’s Attorney have sole enforcement authority for non-DFR entities using Title 9 chapter 63 remedies. Department of Financial Regulation enforces against its licensed/registered entities under applicable financial statutes. Section 2435 does not state a standalone numeric fine.
deadlines: Consumer notice without unreasonable delay, no later than 45 days; preliminary regulator notice within 14 business days or consumer notice, whichever is sooner, subject to statutory exceptions.
amendments: Code history identifies 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2020 amendments. 2025 No. 138 (Adj. Sess.) amendment is explicitly effective January 1, 2027; future text is not treated as current.

title: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act
summary: Establishes consumer data rights, controller and processor duties, and assessments for sensitive or higher-risk processing.
effective: January 1, 2023; later provisions have separate dates.
authority: Virginia Attorney General.
scope: 100,000 consumers annually, or 25,000 consumers and over 50% gross revenue from data sales, subject to statutory scope.
rights: Access, correction, deletion, portability, and qualifying opt-outs from sale, advertising, and significant-effect profiling.
obligations: Provide privacy notices, minimize collection, maintain reasonable security, obtain sensitive-data consent, honor rights and conduct required assessments. Current § 59.1-578(A)(6) prohibits selling or offering to sell precise geolocation data. Known-child processing and location collection carry additional parental-consent and necessity safeguards.
exemptions: Government, specified financial/health entities or data, nonprofits, higher education, and additional statutory exclusions.
penalties: AG exclusive enforcement with injunctions and civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation after the statutory cure process or breach of cure statement. Reasonable investigation expenses and attorney fees recoverable. No private right of action.
deadlines: Requests: 45 days, extendable once by 45 days with timely explanation. Appeal decision: 60 days. AG provides 30 days to cure a noticed violation; a qualifying cure and written assurance prevent that enforcement action.
amendments: Current § 59.1-578 includes 2026 chapter 820 (SB 338), banning sale or offered sale of precise geolocation data. Virginia Division of Legislative Services confirms the signed law in its June 2026 legislative digest. The interactive chaptered-bill page did not expose its text; the amendment-specific effective date still needs direct session-law confirmation. Earlier 2022, 2024 and 2025 amendments also appear in the code histories; minors-related litigation has not been independently reviewed.

2.notes: Unique-identification biometric data is sensitive data requiring consent; comprehensive-law protection.

title: Breach of Personal Information Notification
summary: Requires notice after covered unauthorized access/acquisition with a statutory identity-theft or fraud risk.
effective: July 1, 2008 originally, confirmed by the Virginia Attorney General’s breach-notification requirements document; later amendments have separate histories.
authority: Virginia Attorney General; financial institutions’ primary state regulator has exclusive authority for those entities.
scope: Owners/licensees of computerized resident personal information; special payroll-tax rule.
rights: Qualifying affected residents receive breach notice.
obligations: Notice describes the incident, information involved, protective measures, available assistance number and vigilance advice. Employers/payroll providers have a separate AG reporting duty for qualifying taxpayer-ID/withholding compromises; an incident covered only by that special subsection is excluded from the other section requirements, exemptions and penalties.
exemptions: Qualifying own notification policies, GLBA notification procedures and primary/functional regulator procedures satisfy the specified compliance rules. Bureau of Insurance-regulated entities and specified criminal-intelligence systems are excluded. Good-faith employee acquisition is excluded only if neither misused nor further disclosed; public-record information is excluded. Encryption does not prevent notice when acquired unencrypted or with key access and the statutory fraud-risk condition. Financial institutions are enforced by their primary state regulator.
penalties: Attorney General civil penalty up to $150,000 per breach or similar series found in one investigation; individual direct-economic-damage recovery preserved.
deadlines: Residents and AG: without unreasonable delay, subject to scope/restoration and authorized investigation/security delay. Maintainers notify owners without unreasonable delay; over 1,000 notices trigger credit-agency notice.
amendments: Official history lists 2017, 2019, and 2020 amendments. Special payroll-tax reporting rule applies.

title: Breach of Security of Consumer Information
summary: Requires notice when covered computerized information is accessed and acquired without authorization and the statutory identity-theft or fraud condition is met.
enacted: 2008 enrolled committee substitute for SB 340, passed March 8, 2008.
effective: Ninety days after March 8, 2008 passage; applies to breach discovery or notification on/after effectiveness.
authority: Attorney General exclusive action authority except licensed financial institutions, enforced by their primary functional regulator.
scope: Owners and licensees of covered computerized personal information; maintainers notify the owner/licensee.
rights: Affected residents receive notice explaining information categories and assistance resources.
obligations: Send resident notices and notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies when more than 1,000 people must be notified.
exemptions: Encrypted data can still trigger notice when accessed unencrypted or with a usable key and the harm condition is met.
penalties: AG has exclusive authority except licensed financial institutions, whose primary functional regulator enforces. Civil penalties require repeated and willful violations and may not exceed $150,000 per breach or related series discovered in one investigation. Notice failures are unfair/deceptive practices.
deadlines: Without unreasonable delay, subject to scope/restoration measures and authorized investigation or security delay; maintainers notify owners as soon as practicable.
amendments: Historical versions and subsequent amendments require a separate review.

title: Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Act
summary: Restricts intentional interception and knowing unlawful use or disclosure of wire, oral, and electronic communications.
effective: Ninety days from March 14, 1987 passage, expressly stated in the signed enrolled act.
authority: West Virginia criminal authorities and courts.
scope: Persons intercepting or disclosing covered communications.
rights: Communications protected from unauthorized interception.
obligations: Establish party consent or a qualifying legal authorization.
exemptions: A provider’s good-faith reliance on a court order or legislative authorization is a complete civil/criminal defense under § 62-1D-12(b). Other interception exceptions are specified separately in § 62-1D-3.

title: Notice of Unauthorized Acquisition of Personal Information
summary: Requires covered businesses and Wisconsin government bodies to notify individuals after unauthorized acquisition of covered personal information, including certain biometric information.
effective: March 31, 2006, according to the contemporaneous Wisconsin Commissioner of Insurance November 2006 enacted-legislation bulletin.
authority: Wisconsin enforcement authorities; precise remedies require statutory review.
scope: Businesses operating in Wisconsin and maintaining resident information; also state and local government bodies.
rights: Notice to affected individuals when statutory conditions apply.
obligations: Give notice by mail or an established communication method within the statutory timeframe.
exemptions: No material identity-theft/fraud risk and lawful good-faith employee acquisition exceptions; specified financial and health entities have exclusions.
penalties: A September 23, 2025 federal district-court decision in Negron v.Ascension, following Fox v.Iowa Health System, rejected an independent §134.98 claim while allowing notice failures as evidence supporting negligence. The decision notes contrary out-of-district decisions; it is not presented as a definitive Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling. No statutory fine is inferred from this judicial source.

title: Confidentiality of Patient Health Care Records
summary: Protects patient health care records from release without informed consent or a statutory authorization.
enacted: Confidentiality and access sections 146.82–146.83 trace to 1979 chapter 221; the present remedies section 146.84 traces to 1991 Act 39.
effective: Original §§146.81–146.83: April 30, 1980, calculated from the April 29 publication and the next-day commencement in 1979 chapter 221 §2204; §649t creates those sections without a separate delayed date. This is the original confidentiality/access framework, not a claim that every later remedy began then. The 2025 Act 17 nurse-credential update applies September 1, 2026. The Act 148 fatality-review disclosure amendment takes effect May 1, 2027 (first day of the 13th month beginning after its April 3, 2026 publication).
authority: Wisconsin courts and applicable health/regulatory authorities.
scope: Patient health-care records as defined in §146.81(4), subject to its exclusions and §146.816. Wall v. Pahl (2016 WI App 71) holds that §146.82 does not cover an employee’s mere internal access without disclosure outside the organization; this does not authorize snooping or resolve other privacy/security laws.
rights: Confidentiality and consent-based control over release, subject to authorized disclosures.
obligations: Release records only to authorized people or under valid informed consent and follow redisclosure rules.
exemptions: Section 146.816 exempts HIPAA-covered entities/business associates from §146.82 and specified §51.30 requirements for HIPAA-compliant treatment, payment, health-care operations and specified good-faith serious/imminent-threat disclosures. This is a conditional exemption, not blanket HIPAA immunity. Section 146.82 separately authorizes enumerated releases. Other record types, including §51.30 treatment records and school health records, have separate statutory regimes.
penalties: Section 146.84 permits actual damages, fees and exemplary damages up to $25,000 for knowing/willful violations or $1,000 for negligence, and individual injunctions. Criminal exposure reaches $25,000/nine months for false-pretense acquisition, knowingly unlawful unnecessary disclosure or specified tampering; $100,000/3.5 years for intentional confidential disclosure for financial gain. Negligent disclosure carries up to $1,000 forfeiture. Covered public employees may be suspended/discharged. The section excludes specified nursing-home/facility confidentiality violations; separate law may apply.
deadlines: No universal breach deadline established by this confidentiality provision.
amendments: Confidentiality/access provisions originated in 1979 chapter 221, §649t; §146.84 remedies were created by 1991 Act 39, §2667n. Act 238 of the 2013 session added §146.816’s HIPAA-alignment exception; 2017 Acts 140/143 amend that section. Wall v. Pahl, August 30, 2016, construes the disclosure requirement. 2025 Act 17 §42 updates the nurse credential in §146.82(3)(a)’s driver-fitness disclosure authority, effective September 1, 2026. Enacted 2025 Act 148 (AB 192, approved April 2, 2026) creates fatality-review access and confidentiality rules, including §146.82(2)(d). Section 12 of Act 148 fixes commencement as the first day of the 13th month beginning after publication: May 1, 2027, not an operative November 2026 exception. Complete later-session reconciliation remains open.

title: Genetic Data Privacy

title: Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier
summary: Requires notice and consent before commercial biometric capture, restricts disclosure, and requires reasonable protection and destruction.
enacted: Original HB 678, 2001 chapter 634, signed June 13, 2001, created predecessor §35.50. HB 2278, 2007 chapter 885, recodified it as §503.001; 2007 is not the original biometric-law enactment.
effective: Original law: September 1, 2001 under HB 678 §3. Current numbering: April 1, 2009. HB 149’s AI amendments: January 1, 2026.
authority: Texas Attorney General.
scope: Commercial capture of retina/iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, and hand/face geometry.
rights: Prior notice and consent for commercial capture. An image merely being online is not, by itself, notice/consent unless made public by the individual concerned (§503.001(b-1)).
obligations: Protect stored/transmitted biometrics, restrict disclosures, and destroy after the collection purpose expires.
exemptions: Section 503.001(e) excludes financial-institution/affiliate voiceprints, specified AI model development/training activities unless deployed to uniquely identify a person, and AI security/fraud/integrity investigations. If training identifiers are later used commercially outside these exceptions, possession/destruction requirements and penalties apply. These are conditional exceptions, not an exemption for all AI uses.
penalties: Civil penalty up to $25,000 per violation, sought by Attorney General.
deadlines: Destroy within a reasonable time and no later than one year after the collection purpose expires. Employer collection for security is presumed to end its purpose when employment ends. If another law requires keeping an associated document longer, destruction is due within a reasonable time and at most one year after that retention requirement ends.
amendments: 2001 HB 678 established the predecessor; 2007 HB 2278 recodified it. Amendments: 2009 HB 3186 (chapter 1163; September 1, 2009), 2017 SB 1343 (chapter 913; September 1, 2017), and 2025 HB 149 (chapter 1174; January 1, 2026). Current disclosure, destruction, employer-security and conditional AI rules are summarized separately.

title: California Consumer Privacy Act
summary: A cross-sector consumer privacy framework; sector-specific and statutory exceptions remain important.
scope: Qualifying California for-profit businesses: $26.625 million prior-year gross revenue threshold (adjusted effective 2025); 100,000 residents/households bought, sold, or shared; or at least 50% of revenue from sale/sharing. Related-entity rules also apply.

title: Eavesdropping
summary: Criminalizes unlawful wiretapping, mechanical overhearing, and interception/access of electronic communications.
scope: Defined intentional telephone/telegraph wiretapping, mechanical recording by a person not present, and interception/access of electronic communications without the required participant consent or legal authorization.
rights: CPLR 4506 generally excludes evidence obtained through criminal eavesdropping, with an exception for proceedings against the eavesdropper. An aggrieved participant may seek suppression in a covered civil proceeding.
obligations: Obtain the participant consent required by §250.00 or specific lawful authorization. The one-party rule in these definitions is not permission to intercept unrelated people’s conversations or disregard another jurisdiction’s law.
deadlines: No breach-notification clock is created. A CPLR 4506 civil suppression motion generally precedes the proceeding unless there was no opportunity or the person did not know the grounds.
authority: New York criminal prosecutors
enacted: 1965 Chapter 1030 introduced the revised Penal Law provision, replacing the earlier §738 framework.
effective: Revised Penal Law §250.05 effective September 1, 1967, as shown in the Department of Corrections offense table.
exemptions: The definitions preserve ordinary carrier operation and protection of carrier rights/property. Electronic-communication exclusions include specified public transmissions, tone-only paging and tracking-device communications; lawful CPLArticle 700/705 authorization is distinct.
penalties: Class E felony. Ordinary individual sentencing under §70.00 can carry a maximum prison term of four years, subject to sentencing history and lawful alternatives. A felony fine under §80.00 may reach $5,000 or twice the person’s gain, whichever is greater; corporations are governed separately. This is not an automatic sentence or a statutory civil payout.
amendments: 1988 Chapter 744 added electronic-communication interception/access. That legislative history is independently discussed in the official published Gurevich opinion; current offense wording is published by the Senate. The court opinion is used for amendment history, not as a claim that every access to a stored message violates §250.05.

title: Interception of Wire and Oral Communications
summary: Regulates secret device-based hearing or recording and subsequent disclosure/use.
scope: Covers secret electronic interception of interpersonal conversations and messaging, including modern calls, texts, email and Internet chats, subject to statutory exceptions. In Vita v.NewEnglandBaptistHospital,494Mass 824(2024), the SupremeJudicialCourt held the statute ambiguous as applied to tracking browsing of publicly available hospital webpages and applied lenity to dismiss those claims. The case did not allege interception of patient-portal records or messages to clinicians; it does not establish blanket immunity for all medical tracking or other privacy claims.
rights: Protection against secret recording without required prior all-party authority.
obligations: Avoid prohibited interception, unlawful use/disclosure and possession of devices with unlawful intent.
exemptions: Section 99D permits specified carrier service/protection activities, ordinary business intercoms, federally authorized officers, statutory warrants, undercover-officer/witness safety measures and institutional financial trading calls with semiannual written notice. The officer-safety exception does not make an otherwise unauthorized interception admissible under paragraph P. Paragraph B 4’s officer one-party exception is limited to designated-offense investigations. Separately, the First Circuit in Project Veritas/Martin v. Rollins (2020) held the ban unconstitutional as applied to secret, nonconsensual audio recording of police performing official duties in public. It rejected a facial overbreadth challenge and did not create an unlimited exception for every public official or private conversation.
deadlines: No generic consumer-response/breach clock; civil limitations period not stated in §99Q. Warrant procedures have separate judicial deadlines.
authority: Criminal prosecutors/courts; aggrieved persons civil action under §99Q.
penalties: Interception: up to $10,000 and/or 5 years state prison or 2.5 years jail. Civil §99Q: actual damages at least greater of $100/day or $1,000, punitive damages and reasonable fees/disbursements; good-faith warrant reliance defense.

title: Predictive and Presymptomatic Genetic Testing Consent
summary: Requires informed written consent before covered predictive/presymptomatic genetic tests.
scope: Physicians and delegated practitioners ordering scientifically accepted clinical genetic tests.
rights: Explanation of purpose, limits, risks/benefits, future uses, result notification, access and confidentiality.
obligations: Obtain signed consent before ordering. If using the statutory model, give the subject a signed copy and retain the original medical-record copy. Disclosure duty is bounded by reasonably qualified physician knowledge.
exemptions: §5431 newborn testing and other legal exceptions; qualifying federal-rule biomedical research excluded, as are routine examinations/fluid analyses unless specifically genetic.
deadlines: Consent before ordering; duty began 6 months after March 15, 2000 commencement.
authority: The health-profession licensing department investigates; the appropriate disciplinary subcommittee imposes professional sanctions.
penalties: Section 16221(q) expressly makes a violation of genetic-consent section 17020 or 17520 a disciplinary ground. Section 16226 permits reprimand, probation, suspension, revocation, permanent revocation or fine for that ground. The $250,000 ceiling in section 16226(3) expressly addresses grounds (a) or (b), and is not automatically the fine for a subsection (q) genetic-consent violation. Signing the statutory model consent bars the specified damages action based on failure to obtain informed consent; it is not a general immunity from all wrongdoing.
effective: Immediate March 15, 2000; six-month phase-in for consent duty.
amendments: Current official section history lists 2000 Act 29 without a later amendment.

title: Educational Data: Technology Providers and School Devices
summary: Restricts education technology data sales/commercial use and monitoring of school-issued devices.
scope: Public educational agencies/institutions and contracted technology providers.
rights: Parents/students receive technology-contract notice and may inspect contracts.
obligations: Restrict access, provide safeguards, return/destroy data after contract expiration, and limit device monitoring.
exemptions: No commercial use beyond contracted service; de-identified aggregate improvement permitted. Contract assignment/delegation permitted if transferee bound. Higher-education scope and other subdivision exceptions require separate reading.

Contractor applicability follows §13.05 subd.11, not merely an inference from school obligations.

summary: Prohibits intentional unauthorized interception and knowing use/disclosure of intercepted communications.
scope: Persons intercepting covered communications and public electronic-communications providers.
rights: Communications protected against unlawful interception and disclosure in transit.
obligations: Obtain lawful authority/qualifying consent and respect provider-content disclosure restrictions.
exemptions: Participant/prior one-party consent generally permitted unless criminal/tortious purpose; carrier operations, public radio and legal-process exceptions.

penalties: §362.422 states no independent numeric penalty; it prohibits GLBA-inconsistent disclosure and permits primary state regulators to issue GLBA-consistent rules. Other regulatory remedies require separate governing-law analysis.

title: Employee Social Media Access Restrictions
summary: Limits employer demands for personal social-media credentials, observation and content.
scope: Employers/agents and employees/applicants using password-protected personal accounts.
rights: Refuse unlawful demands without retaliation; seek injunction concerning investigatory demands and small-claims redress.
obligations: Do not request passwords, compelled account access or content except under the statutory investigation test; do not retaliate against refusal or protected speech.
exemptions: Investigations require specific misconduct/proprietary-transfer information or federal/regulatory compliance need, an actual investigation and information necessary for factual determination. Employer devices/business accounts and education-only institution accounts are excluded. Speech protection does not override written employer policy or contract.
deadlines: Small-claims action within 1 year.
authority: Small-claims courts; related communications/privacy and breach enforcement may apply.

summary: Restricts school-service operators’ advertising, profiling, sales and disclosure of student information.
scope: Operators knowingly providing services designed/marketed for elementary, middle or high-school purposes; the definition excludes specified physically present postsecondary institutions.
rights: School-requested deletion, subject to student/parent retention consent; protections against commercial exploitation.
obligations: Maintain reasonable security; delete school-controlled information within reasonable time after school/district request; bind service providers to purpose, redisclosure and security limits.

summary: Restricts intentional interception and knowing use/disclosure of wire, electronic and oral communications.
scope: Persons, communications providers and qualifying workplace monitoring.
rights: Protection against unlawful interception and provider disclosure in transit.
obligations: Use lawful interception authority; give employees reasonable notice when relying on qualifying random performance/service checks.
exemptions: Participant/prior one-party consent unless criminal/tortious purpose; provider necessities, public radio and statutory exceptions.

title: Genetic Information Privacy Act
summary: Controls genetic analysis/information and prohibits specified insurance discrimination.
scope: Persons collecting, analyzing, retaining, transmitting or using genetic material/information under the Act.
rights: Informed written consent; prompt destruction on request subject to exceptions; private civil redress.
obligations: Obtain consent before covered activities and retention; preserve ordinary medical-record protections.
exemptions: Conditioned law enforcement, deceased identification, parentage, newborn screening, deidentified data, registries/research and emergencies. Religious objection limits listed exceptions. title: Physician-Patient Information in Civil Matters
summary: Limits physician disclosure in civil matters of professionally acquired, necessary treatment information that tends to harm the patient’s character.

effective: Chapter 59 effective 60 days after final enactment of April 28, 1978, P.L. 202, No. 53, as the official chapter note states.
authority: Pennsylvania courts applying evidentiary privilege.
scope: Physician testimony in civil matters: information acquired while professionally attending a patient, necessary to that work, and tending to blacken the patient’s character. It is a limited evidentiary privilege, not a comprehensive medical-records privacy statute.
rights: Patient consent is required for disclosure within this narrowly defined privilege unless the statutory exception applies.
obligations: Physicians and litigants must determine whether information falls within the section before disclosure.
exemptions: Patient consent permits disclosure; privilege does not apply in civil personal-injury damages matters brought by the patient.
penalties: The cited section establishes an evidentiary bar to physician testimony and no standalone numeric fine or damages remedy; collateral remedies were not reviewed.
deadlines: This provision is a restriction on testimony during civil proceedings. It imposes no notification or record-request response deadline. Separate causes of action and limitation periods are outside this evidentiary rule.
amendments: Current § 5929 displays no section-specific amendment annotation. Chapter 59’s enactment note establishes codification history; broader privilege case law remains to be reconciled.

title: New York Child Data Protection Act

These are purpose-specific permissions rather than general public availability.
penalties: General Title 32.1 enforcement (§ 32.1-27) makes willful noncompliance a Class 1 misdemeanor unless another penalty applies. The Board/Commissioner may seek judicial compliance orders; violating those orders can carry up to $25,000 per violation, each day separately. That amount is for disobeying the judicial remedy, not an automatic fine for every record disclosure. Private damages require a separately supported cause of action. The related laboratory-results section, §32.1-127.1:06(E), expressly excludes civil, criminal or administrative liability and professional discipline for failing to comply with that section; do not apply the general Title 32.1 penalties to its 72-hour rule.
deadlines: Within 30 days of an authorized copy/electronic-access request, provide access, explain missing records, identify a known holder, or give a permitted denial. General subpoena return dates allow at least 15 days absent a good-cause order; objections generally have 15 days. Following the required certification, records are due on the return date or five days after certification, whichever is later. Other statutory request procedures can govern instead. The related §32.1-127.1:06 generally delays EHR release of finalized pathology/radiology reports reasonably likely to show malignancy and genetic-marker tests for 72 hours. Early release is allowed at the entity’s direction, upon patient/representative request and consent, because system limitations would delay other information, or when the entity/provider determines early release is in the patient’s best interest.
amendments: All 67 chapter references in the current official history were checked against their original enacted texts. Ordinary changes took effect July 1 of their enactment year. Express exceptions: 1998 chapter 470 took effect April 14, 1998; 2003 chapter 907 on March 22, 2003; and 2004 chapters 773/1021 on April 12/21, 2004, under emergency clauses. The relevant amendments in 2011 chapters 798/871 instead took effect July 1, 2012; an earlier July 1, 2011 exception applied to a separate planning duty. The 2000 chapter 813 and 2001 chapter 671 contained July 1, 2001/2003 sunsets, followed by later enactments. Recent substantive changes include 2022 chapter 784: unless the authorization limits it, a designated person may help schedule and attend care appointments; 2025 chapter 182: requested record-change audit trails are included in patient access; and 2026 chapter 248: a separate §32.1-127.1:06 sets the 72-hour EHR release rule for specified malignancy-related reports and genetic-marker results, early-release exceptions and express nonliability for noncompliance. The 67-entry source ledger preserves every approval and commencement date, including the legal basis for default-date inferences.

title: Medical Records Privacy
summary: Texas medical-information privacy extends to a broad range of entities handling protected health information.
effective: Original September 1, 2001; major HB 300 changes September 1, 2012.
authority: Texas Attorney General and applicable licensing agencies.
scope: Broad statutory covered-entity definition includes businesses, schools and information entities handling PHI, subject to chapter exemptions.
rights: Protected health-information confidentiality and limitations on sale and electronic disclosure.
obligations: Appropriate employee training; restrictions on remunerated disclosure and other use/disclosure duties.
exemptions: § 181.051 partially exempts specified insurance entities and employers, while Subchapter D remains applicable. Other specific payment, research and program exceptions require provision-specific application.
penalties: AG injunctions; civil maxima $5,000 negligent, $25,000 knowing/intentional, $250,000 knowing/intentional financial-gain violation. Pattern/practice and statutory mitigation/caps affect awards; licensing discipline may also apply.
deadlines: Electronic records: capable electronic-record providers must supply a requested record within 15 business days after written request, subject to federal access exceptions. Employee training must occur by the 90th day after hiring; material law changes require affected employees’ training within one year. Keep signed training verification for six years.
amendments: Current chapter reflects HB 300, 2015 revisions and later specific exceptions; full session chronology not certified.

title: Student Online Privacy
summary: Restricts educational-service advertising, student profiling and sales; requires safeguards and deletion.
effective: July 1, 2020 under Act 89 §7. Future enforcement amendments and new educational-technology registration rules begin January 1, 2027.

exemptions: General-audience services, connectivity providers and certain intermediary providers are outside specified duties. Educational/adaptive learning, nonidentifying product improvement and permitted research/disclosures remain allowed under §§2443c–e. deadlines: School/district-requested deletion within a reasonable time and where practicable, unless student/parent consents to retention.

deadlines: Sections 60-2-20–21 do not prescribe an administrative filing deadline or special civil limitations period. No general limitations period is asserted from these sections.

amendments: 2003 chapters 965 and 1276 amended/redesignated confidentiality exceptions and authorization provisions.

scope: Employees/employers as defined in §91A.2.
rights: Inspect/copy performance evaluations, discipline and other employment-relations information.
obligations: Provide access at an agreed time; employer representative may attend; copy charges must be reasonable.
authority: Enforcement authority not specified in §91B.1
effective: 1990-07-01 (original Act has no special date; general commencement rule in Iowa Code section 3.7).
deadlines: Employer and employee agree on access timing; section 91B.1 states no fixed number of days.
exemptions: Written employment references are excluded from employee access. An employer representative may attend inspection; reasonable commercial-equivalent copying fees are permitted.
penalties: Section 91B.1 states no standalone fine or express damages formula. Availability of general equitable or other remedies requires separate analysis.
amendments: Original 1990 chapter 1033 section 1; 1998 chapter 1022 section 1 removed the $5 total copying-fee cap and defined reasonable per-page fees; 2008 chapter 1032 section 201 reorganized the section.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Workplace drug-testing confidentiality
summary: Protects records produced by covered workplace drug-testing programs.
scope: Covered employers, laboratories, review officers and assistance/rehabilitation programs handling employee/applicant test information.
rights: Voluntary written consent for disclosures outside statutory exceptions; test information barred from criminal use against tested person.
obligations: Keep testing information confidential; consent identifies recipient, purpose, information, duration and signature.
authority: Florida workers’ compensation/laboratory authorities and competent courts within statutory roles
effective: 1990-07-01 original chapter 90-201 commencement, expressly identified by Florida Supreme Court in Martinez v.Scanlan,582So.2d 1167(1991).
deadlines: Consent before qualifying release; other testing notice/challenge clocks differ and are not represented as general privacy-request deadlines.
exemptions: Specified compelled appeal/disciplinary disclosures, compensability proceedings, and relevant legal-defense consultation.
penalties: §440.102(8) states no separate numeric confidentiality penalty; licensing/benefit/program consequences and independent remedies require separate analysis.
amendments: Original 1990 chapter 90-201 was invalidated prospectively on June 6, 1991 for single-subject defect; court describes 1991 curative reenactments with retroactive July 1, 1990 application. Current 2026 section history includes 1991 chapter 91-1 §13 and later amendments through 2019 chapter 159.
verificationStatus: Published source-backed record; see Sources & Methodology for review scope.

title: Workplace substance-testing confidentiality
summary: Requires confidentiality of covered workplace substance-abuse testing information.
scope: Employers, laboratories, review officers and assistance/rehabilitation programs receiving testing information.
rights: Voluntary written release consent outside statutory disclosures; results not released/used in criminal proceedings against tested employee/applicant.
obligations: Keep records confidential; consent states recipient, purpose, precise information, duration and signature.
authority: Georgia State Board of Workers’ Compensation within drug-free-program framework; courts/state agencies in authorized proceedings
enacted: 1993 Georgia Laws p.1512 §2; Act 558/HB 811, enacting the drug-free workplace program.
effective: July 1, 1993. The Office of Legislative Counsel’s 1993 statutory summary expressly gives this date for Act 558/HB 811, enacting Article 11 of Chapter 34-9, including the confidentiality provision.
deadlines: Consent before qualifying disclosure; section contains no numeric consumer-response clock.
exemptions: Civil/administrative proceedings, state-agency/court compulsion, related licensing discipline and relevant defense counsel consultation have statutory treatment.
penalties: Section 34-9-420(c) makes test information released in violation of its criminal-proceeding restriction inadmissible in that criminal case. The section creates no fixed-dollar fine or express damages formula. Separately, a Board finding that an employer misrepresented compliance with the premium-discount program permits recovery of the discount through additional premiums and policy cancellation under §33-9-40.2(c). Section 34-9-419(e) bars a claim based merely on failure to establish or conduct a testing program; it does not expressly immunize unlawful disclosure. A separate civil damages theory requires its own legal basis and proof.
amendments: Official SBWC-hosted code current through 2024 sessions; 2025–2026 changes not fully reconciled.

title: Employer genetic-screening restrictions
summary: Prohibits employer genetic testing and discriminatory acquisition/use of genetic information.
scope: Employers and employees/prospective employees within Kansas Act Against Discrimination definitions.
rights: Protection against direct/indirect employer genetic screening and discriminatory genetic-information practices.
obligations: Do not subject workers/applicants to genetic tests or seek/use genetic information to discriminate or restrict employment benefits.
authority: Kansas Human Rights Commission; courts following applicable administrative procedures
deadlines: Kansas commission complaint generally within six months of discrimination; continuing-pattern period runs from last act. Certain complaints unresolved after 300 days may be dismissed with administrative exhaustion under §44-1005(i).
exemptions: Act-specific employer/employee definitions and general exceptions require separate application; no genetic-specific exception stated in subsection (a)(9).
penalties: Commission may order cessation, hiring/reinstatement/upgrading and backpay; incidental pain/suffering/humiliation damages capped at $2,000 under §44-1005(k). Court claims require applicable procedural/exhaustion analysis.
amendments: Current 2026 section history lists latest amendment 1999 ch.32 §2, July 1.

title: Wiretap and Communications Privacy
summary: Restricts interception and knowing use/disclosure of intercepted communications.
scope: Persons and public electronic-communication providers; statutory communication definitions apply.
rights: Communications confidentiality and injured-person civil remedy.
obligations: Use lawful authority; consent exception requires participant and prior consent of all parties, without criminal/tortious purpose.
exemptions: Specified law enforcement, carrier operations, emergency/public-radio and legal-process routes; good-faith order/legislative-authorization defense.
penalties: §402(a) felony: up to 5 years and/or $10,000. §410 civil: actual damages at least greater $100/day or $1,000, punitive damages, fees/costs.
deadlines: Consent must precede reliance on the consent exception. Section 10-410 states no separate filing period. Section 5-101 supplies the general three-year period from accrual for civil actions at law unless another Code provision provides otherwise; application of accrual and tolling requires case-specific analysis.
authority: Criminal prosecutors/courts; injured persons under §10-410.
enacted: The present Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Law was enacted by 1977 Chapter 692, section 3, replacing earlier Maryland wiretap provisions. The original act was approved May 26, 1977. The original enacted chapter’s closing page records the approval.
effective: July 1, 1977. Section 4 of the original 1977 Chapter 692 expressly sets that date; the original state archival scan and Maryland appellate opinion in Perry v. State corroborate it.
amendments: The complete effective-date chain for the 39 amendments listed in current §10-402 history is: 1978 Ch.  339 (1978-07-01); 1984 Ch.  442 (1984-07-01); 1985 Ch.  509 (1985-07-01); 1986 Ch.  660/743 (1986-07-01); 1988 Ch.  607 (1988-07-01); 1989 Ch.  5 (1989-03-09); 1989 Ch.  527 (1989-07-01); 1992 Ch.  140 (1992-10-01); 1994 Ch.  105 (1994-10-01); 1997 Ch.  70 §4/343 (1997-10-01); 1998 Ch.  493/524/733 §3 (1998-10-01); 2000 Ch.  288 (2000-10-01); 2002 Ch.  107/213 §6 (2002-10-01); 2004 Ch.  285/539 (2004-10-01); 2005 Ch.  25 (2005-04-12); 2005 Ch.  421/491 (2005-10-01); 2006 Ch.  44 §6 (2006-04-08); 2006 Ch.  300 (2006-10-01); 2011 Ch.  54/55 (2011-10-01); 2012 Ch.  369 (2012-10-01); 2013 Ch.  38/39 (2013-10-01); 2015 Ch.  22 §5 (2015-04-14); 2015 Ch.  128/129 (2015-05-12); 2018 Ch.  145 (2018-06-01); 2019 Ch.  21 §2/22 §2/521 (2019-10-01); 2025 Ch.  608/609 (2025-10-01). These are amendment commencement dates, not all approval dates. Emergency technical legislation accounts for some midyear dates. The 1992 Chapter 140 added a conditional traffic-stop police video-recording exception. The latest 2025 Chapters 608–609 took effect October 1, 2025 and add correctional officers to the conditional body-camera exception. This requires uniform or displayed insignia, reasonable efforts to follow applicable standards, participation in the communication, notice as soon as practicable unless unsafe/impractical/impossible, and a video or digital recording. It is a specific exception, not blanket authority for unannounced recording. Section 10-410’s separate history contains the 1977 original and 1988 Chapter 607 electronic-communications modernization, effective July 1, 1988.

title: Interception and Disclosure of Communications
summary: Prohibits unauthorized interception and knowing disclosure/use.
scope: Wire, oral and electronic communications within statutory definitions.
rights: Protection from unlawful interception and civil redress.
obligations: Obtain at least one party’s consent or statutory authority; avoid knowing unlawful use/disclosure.
exemptions: Civil/criminal good-faith defense for reliance on court order or Attorney General/district-attorney representation under §296(b). Lawful interception and consent exceptions remain governed by §287 and must not be expanded from this defense.
penalties: §15A-296 permits actual damages with a liquidated floor of $100 per violation-day or $1,000, whichever is higher; punitive damages; and reasonable attorney fees/litigation costs. Good-faith reliance on a court order or Attorney General/district-attorney representation is a complete civil and criminal defense under this Article. Criminal §287 classification is separate.
deadlines: Consent before interception; no generic consumer-response clock; civil filing period unresolved.
authority: Criminal prosecutors/courts; injured-person civil action.
enacted: SessionLaws 1995 Chapter 407 section 1, SenateBill 896, ratified July 10, 1995, added sections 15A-286 through 15A-298, including the current interception prohibition and civil remedy.
effective: December 1, 1995, expressly stated in Chapter 407 section 3.
amendments: Current section 15A-287 and civil-remedy section 15A-296 each list 1995 Chapter 407 section 1 as their sole source history. The 1995 original act and current text of these two provisions were compared; other Article 16 provisions have their own histories.

title: Interception and Eavesdropping Restrictions
summary: Restricts intentional wire/oral interception and knowing use/disclosure.
scope: Covered wire/oral communications and secret eavesdropping conduct.
rights: Privacy against unlawful interception/eavesdropping.
obligations: Use statutory authority or qualifying participant/prior-party-consent defense; no crime/unlawful-harm purpose under private-consent defense.
exemptions: Legally authorized acts; specified law-enforcement and private participant/prior-party-consent defenses.
penalties: §12.1-15-02(1) classC felony carries up to 5 years and/or $10,000 for an individual under §12.1-32-01; qualifying secret-loitering/publication under §02(2) classA misdemeanor carries up to 360 days and/or $3,000. Organizational fines have separate §12.1-32-01.1 limits. These are sentencing maxima, not automatic damages.
deadlines: Consent prior to reliance; no general consumer notice clock.
authority: North Dakota criminal prosecutors/courts.
enacted: 1973 SessionLawsChapter 116 section 15, according to the source annotation reproduced in UniCourt’s statutory mirror. This is the adoption of current section 12.1-15-02, not a claim that no predecessor protection existed.
effective: July 1, 1975 for the 1973 criminal-code revision. AttorneyGeneralOpinion 98-04 expressly confirms that SB 2045 commencement was delayed to this date; section 12.1-15-02’s source annotation identifies 1973 Chapter 116 section 15 within that revision.

title: Data Broker Registration
summary: Data brokers must register before covered Oregon collection, sale or licensing and disclose opt-out practices.
effective: Registration required beginning January 1, 2024, confirmed by DFR; act’s emergency enactment date differs from registration start.
authority: Oregon Department of Consumer and Business Services, Division of Financial Regulation.
scope: Statutorily defined businesses collecting and selling/licensing brokered data about Oregon residents.
rights: Public registry transparency about broker contacts and available opt-out choices; registration statute does not itself create a universal deletion/opt-out entitlement.
obligations: Register before covered activities; submit contact information and opt-out declarations; renew annually.
exemptions: Regulated FCRA/GLBA activities; direct customer/employee/donor/investor and similar relationships and their agents; enumerated public-information, publishing, directory, commerce and occasional asset-transfer activities.
penalties: Up to $500 per violation; continuing violation $500 per day; aggregate department penalties capped $10, 000 per calendar year.
deadlines: Register before covered activities; registration expires December 31 of approval year.
amendments: Current 2025 code history lists 2023 chapter 395; chapterwide 2026 amendment notice requires continued targeted update review.

title: Genetic Information Privacy Act: Consumer Testing
citation: Cal. Civ. Code §56.18 et seq.; 2021 Chapter 596 (SB 41)
summary: Protects genetic information held by covered consumer testing companies.
scope: Direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies as defined by §56.18; protected information includes genetic data and associated biological samples.
rights: Request genetic-data deletion and sample destruction; statutory consent protections.
obligations: Provide genetic-data privacy information, obtain required consents, and maintain security procedures.
deadlines: Honor consent withdrawal as soon as practicable, within 30 days; destroy samples within 30 days after withdrawal of storage consent.
authority: Only the specified public prosecutors may bring the chapter’s enforcement action under §56.182(c); it does not create a direct consumer lawsuit.
penalties: Negligent violations: up to $1,000 plus court costs. Willful violations: $1,000–$10,000 plus costs. Each violation is actionable; recovered penalties go to the person whose genetic data is involved.
exemptions: Section 56.184 excludes specified CMIA/HIPAA data and regulated handling, qualifying research, the newborn screening program, and diagnosis-only testing under stated safeguards. Publicly shared consumer information has a separate clause.
enacted: SB 41, 2021 Chapter 596, approved and filed October 6, 2021.
effective: January 1, 2022, applying the regular-session non-urgency commencement rule to the enacted text.
amendments: The official AG-hosted October 26, 2026 entered bankruptcy order (Docket 2768) approved the California settlement after the October 19 announcement. It resolves the specified bankruptcy disputes and sale appeal through conditional payment, dismissals and releases; it is not a general repeal of genetic privacy protections or a merits ruling adopting every party’s interpretation.

title: Private Conversation Eavesdropping
summary: Criminalizes device-assisted eavesdropping on private conversation under statutory definitions.
scope: Private discourse of others; §539a defines eavesdropping and related terms.
rights: Protection against prohibited device-assisted interception of private discourse.
obligations: Do not willfully eavesdrop or knowingly aid/procure unlawful eavesdropping.
exemptions: §539g covers otherwise-lawful official peace-officer activities; common-carrier employees hearing communications in employment; specified utility customer-service recordings with staff awareness and legitimate purpose; employer-property safeguarding surveillance; and corrections telephone monitoring under its separate rules. These exceptions do not resolve participant-recording case-law questions.
penalties: §750.539c criminal exposure: felony up to 2 years and/or $2,000. Separately §750.539h grants parties to unlawfully eavesdropped conversations an injunction, all actual damages against the eavesdropper and court/jury-determined punitive damages; the civil section supplies no fixed punitive schedule.
deadlines: No generic response/breach clock; consent concerns interception itself.
authority: Michigan criminal prosecutors/courts.
amendments: §539h added by 1966 Act 319, effective March 10, 1967. §539g added under that Act and amended 1993 Act 227 effective November 22, 1993; other operative sections require separate historical checking.

summary: Enacted consumer-data framework; operative May 2027.
scope: Alabama-targeted businesses exceeding 25,000 consumers (excluding payment-only data) or 25% gross revenue from data sales.

obligations: Reasonable security, minimization, sensitive-data consent including identifying biometrics/health data; child protections and processor contracts.

penalties: Uncured violations: AG injunction and court-assessed civil penalty up to $15,000 per violation. §11 does not expressly resolve every possible independent private remedy.

title: Access to healthcare records
summary: Patients can obtain their healthcare records and enforce access in court.
scope: Providers licensed by Kansas Board of Healing Arts; patients and authorized recipients.
rights: Receive copies with a signed authorization; revoke authorization in writing.
obligations: Supply copies or explain unavailability within 30 days; observe board-set charge limits.
deadlines: 30 days after authorization; authorization expires within one year.
authority: Kansas courts and Board of Healing Arts
exemptions: Provider may withhold where disclosure reasonably risks substantial harm; §65-6824 also controls.
penalties: Enforcement suit after good-faith conferral; unjustified noncompliance requires costs and free production. Separate board discipline preserved.
amendments: 2026 consolidated history lists 2015 enactment; HB 2683 displayed as introduced, not enacted.

title: Patient medical-record copies
summary: Patients receive one free medical-record copy on written request.
scope: Licensed hospitals and healthcare providers.
rights: First requested copy without charge; subsequent copies capped at $1/page.
obligations: Provide records following written patient request.
deadlines: Section states no numeric response deadline.
authority: Applicable courts/provider regulators; section names no exclusive enforcer
exemptions: Department of Corrections excluded from provider definition; inmate records follow separate rules.
penalties: No standalone numeric penalty or express damages provision in this section; other remedies not reconciled.

title: Patient access and healthcare-record retention
summary: Provides access, copying limits and retention rules for healthcare records.
scope: Defined private/state providers and qualifying laboratories/facilities; authorized requestors.
rights: Copies of treatment records and transmitted patient information; requested digital format where held digitally.
obligations: Provide authorized copies and requested completeness certification without an extra certification charge. Paper-record copies: up to $1/page for the first 25 pages, $0.50/pages 26–350, then $0.25/page; one handling charge up to $25 and actual postage. Digital-record copies capped at $100 plus actual postage; digital imaging copies capped at $200 plus postage. Imaging handling charges are $20 for hospitals/$10 for others. Do not divide record-type requests to multiply handling charges. Physicians/dentists retain medical records at least six years after last treatment and diagnostic images at least three years, longer on written patient request.
deadlines: Copies within reasonable time, maximum 15 days after request/authorization. Enforcement clauses separately specify 3-day correction,15-day penalty trigger and 5-day final notice.
authority: Louisiana courts
effective: Original commencement unresolved; current operative section reviewed.
exemptions: Harm/safety denial; specified Social Security examinations excluded. Gross-negligence and compliant-test-release liability rules apply.
penalties: Specified copy-rule violations: $500/violation plus discretionary fees/costs after statutory notice. Delayed production can require fees/expenses after certified notice and failure to produce within 5 days.
amendments: Redesignated 2015 from 40:1299.96; displayed latest amendment 2021 Act 277.

title: Mental-health information confidentiality
summary: Limits disclosure and redisclosure of identifiable mental-health treatment information.
scope: Mental-health professionals, facilities, data collectors, agents and recipients.
rights: Voluntary written authorization, inspection of disclosed information and written revocation.
obligations: Record disclosure date/recipient; notify recipients of restrictions; payor safeguards and destruction when no longer needed.
deadlines: Authorization specifies duration; no general numeric consumer-response clock.
authority: Iowa courts/prosecutors; Insurance Commissioner receives payor safeguard statements
effective: 1986-04-23 original commencement after both required publications; Secretary of State certification records April 21 and April 23 publications.
exemptions: Conditional care coordination, emergencies, mandatory reporting, proceedings, payor/peer review and family-care disclosures.
penalties: Section 228.7(3) makes willful unlawful use/disclosure by third-party-payor or peer-review employees/agents a serious misdemeanor, with a special fine up to $500 for the first offense or $5,000 for each later offense, notwithstanding ordinary misdemeanor sentencing. This special penalty is not a general fine for every chapter violation. Section 228.2 warns civil damages or criminal penalties may apply. In Doe v.Central Iowa Health System,766N.W.2d 787(Iowa 2009), the Supreme Court expressly assumed without deciding that §228.2 implied a private claim; it rejected recovery for insufficient causal proof. That decision does not establish or reject a general statutory private cause of action.
amendments: The 2026 Code incorporates 2024 chapter 1170 §506 in the definitions and 2024 chapter 1161 §§71,137 in compulsory disclosures; the latter amendment applies July 1, 2025. The published Code still cites repealed §230A.108 and explicitly warns that corrective legislation is awaited. The Legislature’s 2026 Code-and-Acts Sections Amended report contains no Chapter 228 entry. The defunct cross-reference is disclosed as a source-text defect, not presented as an independent current disclosure authorization.

summary: Patients and authorized representatives can obtain medical records.
scope: Healthcare providers defined in §671-1; living patients and specified deceased-patient representatives.
rights: Access copies; attorney access if direct patient release would harm health; deceased-patient written instructions respected.
obligations: Give complete accurate copies to properly authorized attorney; reasonable copying costs borne by requestor.
deadlines: Authorized attorney request: reasonable time, maximum 10 working days. This clock is not expressly applied to every direct patient request.

title: Patient-record confidentiality, access and security
summary: Protects patient records and permits patient access under defined disclosure rules.
scope: Defined records owners/custodians and practitioners; chapter 395 licensed facilities excluded.
rights: Timely treatment-record copies; written authorization generally controls external disclosures and marketing.
obligations: Security/confidentiality procedures, staff training, disclosure logs and restrictions on redisclosure; notice on practice closure/relocation.
deadlines: Patient copies timely without legal-review delay; specific child-protection department requests within 14 days.
authority: Licensing authorities; Attorney General for unlicensed records owners

penalties: Licensees subject to discipline; AG injunction and fines up to $5,000/violation for records owners not otherwise state-licensed.

title: Patient access, transfer and confidential disposal of medical records
summary: Gives patients record-copy and transfer rights and safeguards records when physicians leave practice.
scope: Persons certified to practice medicine and specified estate representatives.
rights: Obtain copies under board fee schedule; request transfer to another physician; sue for damages/injunction.
obligations: Notify affected patients before ending services; preserve records for applicable seven-year periods; dispose confidentially.
deadlines: Copy request: 45 days from record closure/complete assembly unless medically necessary sooner. Discontinuation notice at least 30 days beforehand.
authority: Delaware Board of Medical Licensure and Discipline; courts
effective: Original §1761 took effect on enactment July 17, 1984: original Act contains no delayed commencement clause, and the Legislature’s glossary states that Delaware Acts normally take effect on enactment unless otherwise specified. exemptions: Specified referral physicians and hospitals/agencies excluded; compliant disposal immunity; disability-benefits requests exempt from advance-payment rule.
penalties: Violations may be unprofessional conduct; aggrieved patient/representative expressly may seek civil damages, injunction or both.
amendments: 2023 ch 161 revised discontinuation notices, approved August 9, 2023; current code history reviewed.

title: Direct-to-consumer genetic data privacy
summary: Protects consumer genetic information through consent, privacy notices, access/deletion tools and security duties.
enacted: 2026 chapter 164 (SB 49), signed March 23, 2026, as shown by the signed session law and Attorney General’s contemporaneous March 23 announcement. A differing bill-index date is not used as the signing date.

title: Mental-health treatment confidentiality
summary: Protects identifying communications and information obtained during mental-health treatment or evaluation.

authority: Courts apply statutory disclosure and authorization rules; these two sections identify no dedicated enforcement agency.

exemptions: Specified involuntary-examination proceedings, a court relevance/confidentiality balancing order, authorized background-check reporting, imminent-injury protection, HIPAA-authorized disclosure and designated guardianship proceedings.
penalties: Sections 27-3-1 and 27-3-2 contain no fixed monetary fine or damages schedule. A private tort action for violating section 27-3-1 is judicially recognized: Allen v. Smith (1988), reaffirmed in Barber v. Camden Clark Memorial Hospital (2018), syllabus point 4. Recoverable amounts depend on the established tort and injury; the decisions reviewed do not supply an automatic per-disclosure award.
deadlines: Signed authorization precedes consent-based disclosure. Thompson v. amendments: Official signed 1977 SB 585 contains article 3 confidentiality text. Current § 27-3-1 also links 2007, 2008, 2017 and 2018 acts; § 27-3-2 has its own consent history. Original predecessor chronology is distinguished from the confirmed 1977 version.

title: Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Privacy
summary: Prohibits purposeful unlawful interception, disclosure or use of protected communications.
scope: Wire, electronic and oral communications within statutory definitions; exceptions depend on the actor and circumstances.
rights: A person whose communications are unlawfully intercepted, disclosed or used may sue under section 24.
obligations: Do not purposefully intercept, procure interception or knowingly use/disclose intercepted communications outside an authorized exception.
exemptions: A private participant or person with one party’s prior consent may record absent prohibited criminal, tortious or injurious purpose. Being a telephone subscriber does not authorize recording other parties’ conversations. Carrier operations, specified official investigations, public-access electronic communications and listed radio activities have distinct exceptions. Disclosure/use prohibitions exclude common-knowledge/public information.
deadlines: Consent must precede interception when the consent exception is used. The federal district court decision Sweeten v. Middle Township, December 14, 2007, pages 15–18, applies NewJersey’s two-year personal-injury limitation under 2A: 14-2 to a 2A: 156A-24 claim, with discovery-rule accrual when the claimant knew or reasonably should have known the actionable facts. Claims against public entities may also face separate TortClaims Act notice requirements; the decision discusses 90-day notice and late-notice relief. Section 24 itself does not state this limitation.
authority: Criminal prosecutors and courts; injured persons’ civil actions under section 24.
penalties: Section 3 classifies prohibited conduct as a third-degree crime. Section 24 provides actual damages with a floor equal to the greater of $100 per violation-day or $1,000, punitive damages, reasonable fees and litigation costs.

rights: Claimant identity and claim records are generally nonpublic. Authorized access and the limited journalist provision remain available.
obligations: Obtain required authority before examining files; do not forge authorization or solicit unauthorized access. Agency personnel must respect disclosure restrictions. Recipients may not recklessly misuse protected information for nonjournalistic disclosure or solicitation of representation.
exemptions: Authorized agency, claimant or employer access; permitted agency statistical publications; specified proceedings involving the agency; and qualifying signed journalist requests. The journalist exception excludes disclosures revealing claims arising from coerced sexual conduct.
deadlines: Authority must precede file examination. This section states no fixed general claimant-access response deadline.
authority: Bureau and Commission administer access; criminal prosecutors and courts enforce the expressly incorporated offense.
penalties: Section 4123.99(D) makes a 4123.88 violation a second-degree misdemeanor. For an individual,2929.24(A)(2) permits up to 90 days in jail and 2929.28(A)(2)(a)(ii) permits a fine up to $750; other authorized sentencing sanctions may apply. This is not a damages schedule automatically payable to claimants.
enacted: Historical predecessor: 1931, 114 Ohio Laws 789, 791, as documented by the Sixth Circuit in Bevan & Associates v. Yost (2019). The 1953 codification preceded the 2006 addition of divisions (B)–(E), including explicit nonpublic-record and journalist provisions. Current version: 2021 H.B.75.
effective: September 28, 2021 for the current version, expressly identified by the official code page.
amendments: The 2006 legislation added divisions (B)–(E), distinct from the older unauthorized-access language. The official version list includes 2007 HB 9, 2008 SB 334, September 7, 2021 SB 4 and September 28, 2021 HB 75. In 2019, Bevan & Associates v. Yost held the then-worded blanket solicitation prohibition unconstitutional; the court distinguished that speech restriction from separate disclosure/access restrictions. Read the current 2021 text rather than treating every phrase of the 2019 version as present enforceable law.

title: Synthetic Sexual Images and Harmful AI Offenses
summary: Prohibits specified nonconsensual sexual deepfakes and intentionally harmful AI systems.
authority: Criminal prosecution; courts.
scope: Knowing harmful distribution, promotion or benefit-seeking threats involving identifiable sexual deepfakes; purpose-built child-pornography or self-harm AI systems.
rights: Protection from specified nonconsensual intimate synthetic material. Consent to creation or prior transmission alone does not excuse prohibited distribution.
obligations: Do not distribute prohibited material or intentionally develop/distribute systems designed for prohibited child-pornography or self-harm uses. Using AI is no defense to a criminal charge.
exemptions: Section 307 preserves service-provider protections for others’ content. Sections 308/701 exclude specified incidental user-prompt output, educational/library and law-enforcement/judicial activities; 701 also excludes legitimate licensed treatment. Developer civil immunity is separately qualified by knowledge/intent of an illegal primary purpose.
penalties: Sexual deepfake distribution: up to 10 years/$10,000; repeat up to 12 years/$10,000. Prohibited child-pornography/self-harm AI systems: up to 10 years/$10,000. Each is a felony; imprisonment and fine may both apply. Sections 307–308/701 do not state a separate fixed civil award.
deadlines: No separate notice/cure window in these offense provisions; conduct and offense-date rules govern.
amendments: HB 0102 also amends child-pornography definitions and offenses; this record focuses on newly created provisions.

title: Police Drone Surveillance and Biometric Matching Limits
summary: Restricts police drone surveillance and forbids facial recognition or other biometric matching on drone data about people, homes or areas outside the surveillance target.
effective: October 1, 2016, expressly stated in the current section’s history.
authority: Law enforcement agencies; courts assess warrants and admissibility.
scope: Vermont police agencies and entities acting on their behalf, as defined in § 4621.
rights: Limits collection about non-targets and protects peaceful speech and assembly from prohibited drone data gathering or retention.
obligations: Operate permitted drones to collect only target data and avoid other people, homes and areas. Do not apply facial recognition or biometric matching to non-target data.
exemptions: Noncriminal purposes such as rescue and disaster assessment; warrants and judicially recognized warrant exceptions. Speech/assembly subsection permits observation without data gathering or retention and warranted uses.
penalties: Illegally gathered information or evidence is inadmissible in judicial or administrative proceedings. Section 4622 specifies no monetary penalty or private damages formula.
deadlines: For an exigent-circumstances drone use, obtain a warrant within 48 hours after use begins. If denied, stop immediately and destroy the resulting information or evidence.
amendments: Current official history lists Act 169, section 2; no later amendment is listed for this section.

effective: July 1, 2001, expressly stated in § 146a.44 and the official source note. Selected amendments effective August 10, 2019.
authority: Pennsylvania Insurance Commissioner and Insurance Department.
scope: Licensees handling nonpublic personal financial information for personal, family or household insurance products/services, including relevant claimants and beneficiaries; generally excludes commercial/agricultural and company information.
rights: Privacy notice; opt out of non-exempt nonaffiliate disclosures; protection against unfair discrimination for opting out.
obligations: Provide initial/revised notices and required annual notices; honor opt-outs. Restrict recipients’ onward sharing/use according to the original disclosure basis.
exemptions: Conditional service-provider/joint-marketing and transaction-servicing exceptions; consent, fraud prevention, legal requirements/process and other § 146a.33 exceptions. Annual notice excused only where unchanged practices and permitted-exception sharing satisfy § 146a.12(b).
penalties: Section 146a.43 invokes applicable Unfair Insurance Practices Act remedies. That Act authorizes cease-and-desist, injunctions and conditional license action. When § 11 predicates are satisfied, court penalties include up to $5,000 per knowing/reasonably-knowable violation ($50,000 per six months), $1,000 otherwise ($10,000 per six months), and $10,000 per violation of an effective commissioner order. These are cross-referenced conditional maxima, not automatic awards to customers. Separate claims must satisfy their own statutory or common-law requirements.
deadlines: Ordinarily annual notice at least once per 12 consecutive months. Before non-exempt disclosure, allow reasonable opt-out opportunity; § 146a.21 gives 30-day mailed/electronic examples and a transaction-specific alternative. Honor choices under the notice rules; no general consumer-access response clock established here.
amendments: Current official chapter shows 2019 amendments to purpose, definitions, notices and safe harbor, including annual-notice exception.

title: Digital Forgery of an Identifiable Person
summary: Criminalizes generating/creating and distributing a deceptive forged digital likeness as genuine with specified fraudulent or injurious intent.
effective: 60 days after approval: September 5, 2025 (calculated from the enacted 60-day clause).
authority: Criminal prosecutors and courts.

title: Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act
summary: Future law requiring AI disclosures in advertising that misrepresents the advertised goods or services.

title: Wire, Oral and Electronic Communications Interception
summary: Limits unauthorized interception and disclosure of private communications, with a one-party-consent exception and civil remedies.
scope: Section 501 covers telephone communications, including cellular and cordless calls; private electronic signals; and oral communications made with a justified expectation against interception. The article also regulates court-authorized Bureau of Narcotics wiretaps.
rights: An affected person can sue those who unlawfully intercept, disclose, use or arrange interception. Section 525 provides suppression procedures for unlawful or improperly authorized evidence and protections for identified nonsuspects.
obligations: Use a valid statutory exception or required court authorization before interception. Subsequent disclosure has its own limits; lawful recording does not authorize unrestricted redistribution. Privileged communications retain their privileged character under §511.
exemptions: Section 531 excludes qualifying carrier service/protection and business-improvement activities, authorized technical assistance, and interception by a party or with one party’s prior consent. For private actors, the consent exception does not cover a criminal, tortious or other injurious purpose. Good-faith reliance on a court order is a civil/criminal defense under §529.
deadlines: Judicial inventory notice ordinarily follows within 90 days after denial or order/extension expiry; a judge may postpone for good cause, but evidence cannot be disclosed at trial before service. Section 525 generally requires court-order/application copies at least 10 days before a proceeding, subject to judicial waiver, and suppression motions before trial unless earlier opportunity or knowledge was lacking.
authority: State prosecutors and criminal courts enforce §533. Aggrieved people bring civil actions under §529. Judicial supervision governs authorized narcotics interception and suppression.
penalties: Section 533: knowing intentional unlawful device possession/installation/operation/monitoring is a misdemeanor, up to one year in county jail or $10,000, or both. Violating §511 disclosure/use limits is a felony, up to five years and a fine up to $10,000. Section 529 allows actual damages with a minimum of $100 per day or $1,000, whichever is higher, plus punitive damages, reasonable attorney fees and litigation costs.
enacted: Original 1989 chapter 553 was subject to repeal; the framework was enacted again in 1992 chapter 561 and amended in 1995 chapter 520. The official Legislature confirms the 2004 chapter 511 reenactment was approved May 4, 2004.
effective: The confirmed 2004 reenactment took effect July 1, 2004. Chapter 379 of 2006 removed the sunset provision on March 13, 2006, effective on passage. Earlier original operative dates require historical verification; this record does not treat 2004 as the first adoption.
amendments: The reviewed statutory history identifies 1999 Chapter 403 (consent exceptions), 2004 Chapter 511 (reenactment), 2005 Chapter 463 (definitions), and 2006 Chapter 379/SB 2744 (repeal of §537’s sunset, not the substantive interception protections). The 2026 regular-session code-affected index was checked for all twenty listed article sections, §§501–537: its sole measure was SB 2331 affecting §513, which died in committee February 3. No enacted amendment to these existing article sections was identified in that official index. This finding is limited to the specified sections and session.

title: Insurance Information Privacy and Marketing Disclosures
summary: Provides insurance-record access and correction, limits disclosure and marketing uses, and supplies targeted private remedies.
scope: Insurance institutions, agents and insurance-support organizations handling covered insurance transactions. Life, health and disability coverage protects residents; property/casualty and mortgage-guaranty coverage use the State-issued/delivered/renewed policy connection. Credit insurance is included. This is insurance-sector legislation, not a general broker registry.
rights: Request access/copies and institutional sources under §45; request correction, amendment or deletion under §50 and attach a disagreement statement if refused. Obtain reasons and supporting information for an adverse underwriting decision under §55. Section 75(11) allows refusal of specified third-party marketing disclosures; medical, privileged and character/habit information cannot use that marketing route.
obligations: Give required information-practice notices; limit disclosure to an authorized statutory route; honor marketing objections; carry dispute statements forward in later disclosures. Section 75 requires written authorization unless another enumerated disclosure exception applies. An affiliate marketing exception cannot disclose medical-record information.
exemptions: Public records maintained to insure real-property title are excluded. Access/correction rights have exclusions for anticipated claims or litigation and consumer-reporting agencies. Authorized disclosure routes include necessary business/insurance functions, fraud prevention, medical verification/audits, regulators, legal process, conditioned research, business transfers, and specified government/benefit purposes. These are conditional routes, not permission for unrestricted onward sale. Section 110 protects compliant disclosures/furnishing, but not malicious or willfully injurious false information.
deadlines: Access and correction responses: 30 business days. For underwriting reasons, submit a written request within 90 business days after notice; response is due within 21 business days. A §105 suit must start within two years after the violation was or should have been discovered. Marketing-disclosure notices have separate rules, including §27(g)’s 30-day advance notice for qualifying group-policy disclosure under §75(11).
authority: Insurance Commissioner investigates and issues cease-and-desist orders under §§80–95. Individuals may seek the specific Superior Court relief authorized by §105; this is not a private remedy for every Article 39 breach.
penalties: Section 105 permits equitable relief for access/correction/underwriting-right violations and actual damages for unlawful §75 disclosure; recovery cannot exceed actual loss. Courts may award costs and reasonable fees to the prevailing party. Section 95 permits civil penalties under §58-2-70, ordinarily $100–$1,000 with each day separately counted under that provision. Violating a cease-and-desist order can bring court-imposed fines up to $10,000 per violation or $50,000 for a general business practice, and license suspension/revocation. Knowingly obtaining information by false pretenses is a Class 1 misdemeanor under §115.
enacted: Chapter 846 §1, ratified July 7, 1981, created the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act, originally Article 34. Later codification places it in Article 39.
effective: Original act generally effective July 1, 1982; its §58-404 expressly began access, correction and disclosure rights January 1, 1982 regardless of collection date. The 2025 funeral-information exception amendment applies to inquiries 30 days after July 9, 2025 approval; this relative statutory period is retained without presenting the act’s other October dates as its start.
amendments: Reviewed changes: 1985 chapter 666 §68 added authorized DMV disclosure (effective ratification July 10, 1985); 1997-443 §11A.20A renamed the immunization recipient department to Health and Human Services; 2001-351 aligned notice/disclosure with federal financial privacy; 2003-262 reorganized the article and added security safeguards; 2009-566 §24 added funeral-service inquiry disclosure, effective October 1, 2010; 2025-76 §2.3(b) expanded that cross-reference. Current §75 also lists 1993 chapter 134 §2; its archived operative text could not be retrieved, so the entire historical chain is not certified complete.
