title: Book, Music and Video Customer Privacy
summary: Restricts disclosure of identifiable media-purchase/rental/borrowing records and gives customers a marketing opt-out.
scope: Retail sellers, renters and lenders of books or other written materials, sound recordings and video recordings, including their employees/agents. A customer is an individual buying, renting or borrowing covered material. This is a media-record rule, not a general data-broker registry.
rights: Receive notice of the marketing-disclosure opt-out and request removal of one’s name. The current civil remedy requires actual harm; it does not supply an automatic $5,000 payment for a current violation.
obligations: Do not knowingly disclose identifiable covered customer records without a permitted route. Marketing notices must explain removal methods; a nonelectronic method is required unless communication with customers is electronic. Conspicuous online privacy notices may qualify.
exemptions: Aggregated or otherwise non-identifiable records fall outside §1712. Section 1713 allows written customer permission, warrants/court orders, necessary overdue-payment collection after notice, grand-jury subpoenas and conditioned marketing. Its ordinary-business exception covers records created or obtained after July 31, 2016; this cutoff must not be omitted.
deadlines: For the marketing exception, the prohibition on knowingly disclosing the opted-out customer’s name begins 30 days after receipt of the customer’s notice. The Act sets no separate consumer access/deletion-response process. It does not state a dedicated civil filing period in §1715.
authority: State criminal prosecutors/courts enforce the misdemeanor. Customers with actual damage may bring the private civil action in §1715, independently of prosecution.
penalties: Violation is a misdemeanor under §1714. Current §1715 permits actual damages, including emotional distress, plus reasonable costs and attorney fees; lawful disclosures permitted by §1713 create no liability. Section 1714 supplies no numeric fine or incarceration term in its own text.
enacted: 1988 Public Act 378 created the media-privacy prohibitions. 1989 Public Act 206 added the private civil action.
effective: Original Act: March 30, 1989. Private civil-action section: November 7, 1989. Current 2016 Public Act 92 amendments: July 31, 2016, as expressly recorded in official section histories.
amendments: The reviewed official section histories list the 1989 addition of §1715 and the 2016 amendments to §§1711–1715. The 2016 changes added the non-identifiable-data and ordinary-business provisions, revised the marketing notice/opt-out process, and replaced the earlier $5,000 statutory floor with an actual-damages requirement. The legislature described the amendment as curative; that label is not treated here as resolving every historical claim’s retroactivity.

title: Insurance Financial and Health Information Disclosure
summary: Insurance-sector rules require authorization for specified information sharing, subject to exceptions.
scope: Insurance licensees; personal/family/household financial information and nonpublic health information. Business/commercial/agricultural financial transactions are excluded.
rights: Authorize or refuse covered disclosure; revoke authorization; receive privacy notices. This is not a general broker-registration law.
obligations: Obtain required authorization before nonaffiliated financial sharing; restrict reuse and account-number marketing; follow health-disclosure rules.
exemptions: Conditional exceptions cover servicing, joint marketing, fraud, legal process and specified insurance functions. HIPAA compliance substitutes for specified health-rule provisions.
deadlines: Initial notice generally at relationship formation; annual notice means each twelve-month period, subject to exceptions. Health authorizations last at most 24 months and are revocable.
authority: Insurance Commissioner implements §26.1-02-27. Commissioner may seek injunctions through the Attorney General under §26.1-02-09.
penalties: Section 26.1-02-27 expressly creates no private action. Under §26.1-01-03.3, title violations generally allow administrative fines up to $10,000 per violation after hearing and restitution of direct financial loss. The Commissioner cannot adjudicate or order payment of a disputed policy claim through that restitution power.
enacted: Administrative rules adopted effective December 1, 2001 under §26.1-02-27; this records rule adoption rather than claiming a separate legislative enactment.
effective: Original rule December 1, 2001; revised authorization framework November 1, 2004. Annual-notice amendment April 1, 2021.
amendments: Official rule histories identify 2004 disclosure changes and the 2021 annual-notice exception. The current statute prohibits annual-notice requirements when compliant third-party sharing and unchanged practices meet its exception. The 2025 HB 1088 general penalty amendment adds per-violation fines and bounded restitution.

title: Interception and recording of communications
summary: Generally requires participation or consent from at least one party to intercept and record covered communications.
scope: Wire, landline, oral, telephone and wireless communications; recording or possessing the resulting recording is covered.
rights: A participant may record; an outsider normally needs prior consent from a participant. Other privacy and federal laws can impose additional limits.
obligations: Do not intercept and record, or possess a recording, outside the statutory consent rule or an applicable exception.
deadlines: Consent must precede the covered interception; this section supplies no general consumer access-request period.
authority: Arkansas criminal prosecutors and courts
enacted: Act 1006/HB 1450, approved April 12, 1993, as printed on the official act’s final page. Sections 1–5 establish the substantive rule; sections 6–8 address codification, severability and conflicting laws.
effective: August 13, 1993: the full eight-section act contains no emergency or special commencement clause. The Bureau of Legislative Research’s official session-date table identifies August 13 as the 1993 regular-session default, citing Attorney General Opinion 93-149A. Applying that default is an explicit legal inference.
exemptions: Persons acting under color of law and specified assistance; necessary ordinary-course carrier functions, telecommunications services, licensed amateur-radio activity, and pleasure police-scanner use. Stored-content and pen-register court procedures have separate rules.
penalties: A violation is a Class A misdemeanor. This section does not itself specify a fixed consumer civil award.
amendments: Source history lists 2001 Acts 1190,1773,1823 and 2003 Act 1087 §7.

title: Wiretapping and eavesdropping protections
summary: Colorado restricts nonconsensual interception of communications and eavesdropping on private conversations.
scope: Wire/electronic communications and private conversations under the separate statutory offenses.
rights: Consent of a sender or receiver generally permits covered interception; private conversation recording generally requires consent of a principal party.
obligations: Do not knowingly intercept, unlawfully use or disclose intercepted communications, or assist prohibited conduct.
deadlines: Consent and applicable authorization must exist when interception occurs; these provisions contain no general consumer request clock.
authority: Colorado criminal prosecutors and courts
enacted: Original wiretapping/eavesdropping framework: 1967 SB 116, approved April 26, 1967, as recorded in the Legislative Reference Office official 1967 enacted-bill digest. Repealed and reenacted within the 1971 criminal code.
effective: Original SB 116 took effect April 26, 1967. The 1971 criminal-code repeal-and-reenactment applies to offenses on or after July 1, 1972 under §18-1-103(1)–(2). Current Class 2 misdemeanor classification applies from March 1, 2022; §303 also has an October 1, 2023 amendment.
exemptions: Authorized law-enforcement activity, defined ordinary carrier operations, publicly accessible transmissions and other specified exceptions. Own-premises security/business surveillance requires reasonable public notice; news-gathering exceptions are qualified. Good-faith court-order reliance is a defense under the statutory conditions.
penalties: Class 2 misdemeanor: for offenses on or after March 1, 2022, up to 120 days jail, a fine up to $750, or both under §18-1.3-501. Do not treat this criminal limit as an automatic civil damages award.
amendments: §303 history includes 2021 SB 21-271 §330 effective March 1, 2022 and 2023 HB 23-1293 §40 effective October 1, 2023. §304 includes SB 21-271 §331 effective March 1, 2022.

title: Private communications interception
summary: Georgia protects private communications and generally permits audio interception with one party’s consent.
scope: Clandestine interception of private conversations and messages; private-place visual surveillance is separately regulated and cannot be justified solely by the audio one-party rule.
rights: A party to a wire, oral or electronic communication, or a person with a party’s prior consent, receives the §66(a) exception.
obligations: Avoid clandestine interception outside consent or a statutory authorization. Private video ordinarily requires consent of all persons observed, subject to its separate statutory conditions and exceptions.
deadlines: Consent must precede interception; no general access-request clock is created.
authority: Georgia criminal prosecutors and courts
enacted: April 19, 1967: Act 567/HB 64, Georgia Laws 1967 pp 844–852, replacing Code Chapter 26-20. The later 1968 Criminal Code and 1982 recodification are distinct events.
effective: April 19, 1967 for the 1967 framework (legal inference). The complete Act 567 contains no delayed commencement; under the pre 1969 rule explained in Jones v.Caldwell, an act without a later date took effect upon approval. The 1968 default-date statute applied to acts approved after January 1, 1969 and is not retroactively applied here.
exemptions: §66 includes court-authorized and narrowly defined parent/child telephone-monitoring rules; these do not authorize every parental interception or unrestricted disclosure. Separate visual-surveillance exceptions and constitutional requirements must be assessed independently.
penalties: §69 generally makes violations felonies punishable by 1–5 years imprisonment, a fine up to $10000, or both, subject to its specified exception. §67 generally excludes illegally obtained evidence in Georgia courts except proceedings proving a violation of this part.
amendments: §62 source history includes 2015 SB 94 and 2022 SB 539/SB 10; §66 history includes 1993, 1994 and 2000 amendments.

title: Electronic communications interception
summary: Indiana restricts unauthorized interception of electronic communications and provides a civil remedy for unlawful interception, use or disclosure.
scope: Intentional acquisition or recording of electronic communications by an outsider without the sender’s or receiver’s consent; includes computer and fax communications. Do not assume this statutory definition covers every unaided in-person conversation.
rights: Consent from either the sender or receiver generally takes the conduct outside the statutory interception definition. An affected person may sue for qualifying violations.
obligations: Do not knowingly or intentionally intercept covered communications unlawfully. Criminal-justice personnel also face the separate prohibited-use/disclosure provision.
deadlines: Civil claim generally must be brought within 2 years after interception, disclosure or use initially occurs, whichever is later; the text is not a discovery-based period.
authority: Indiana criminal prosecutors and courts; affected persons through civil actions
enacted: Article added by P.L.161-1990 §3; definition relocated by P.L.114-2012 §67.
effective: July 1, 1990. The Seventh Circuit expressly identifies this commencement date in Davis v. Zirkelbach, 149 F.3d 614 (1998), and applies it to reject a claim based on a May 1990 interception. Later disclosure did not turn that earlier recording into an interception governed by the new act.
exemptions: Federally authorized interception is excluded from §5 criminal prohibition. The definition excludes specified public radio transmissions. Good-faith warrant reliance is a civil defense; qualifying journalists have a narrowly conditioned affirmative defense.
penalties: Unlawful interception is a Level 5 felony. Civil relief under §4 includes greater of actual damages or statutory damages of $100 perday or $1000, plus appropriate punitive damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees. Awards depend on the statutory claim and court findings.
amendments: Civil section history includes P.L.1-1998 §194 and P.L.106-2010 §9; criminal classification amended by P.L.158-2013 §388. Definition moved in 2012.

title: Communications Interception and Privacy Remedies
summary: Restricts unauthorized telephone interception and provides court-supervised interception procedures and civil remedies.
scope: Section 30-12-1 covers knowing, unauthorized interference with telegraph and telephone communications, lines and equipment. Its text is not a general ban on recording every face-to-face conversation or every online activity.
rights: People whose wire or oral communications are intercepted, disclosed or used contrary to the Act can bring a civil action. Aggrieved parties may seek suppression for unlawful interception, a deficient order or interception outside its terms.
obligations: Court orders must identify the target if known, facilities or place, communication type, offense, authorized agency and interception period. Authorized officers may share information with other officers only as appropriate to official duties; properly obtained communications may be disclosed in criminal or grand-jury testimony.
enacted: The interference section originates in 1963 Chapter 303 §12-1; 1973 Chapter 369 established the court-order and civil-remedy framework.
effective: The reviewed reproductions identify enacted years but do not establish original calendar commencement. No day is inferred from a default rule without the underlying session-law text.
authority: State criminal courts and prosecutors administer the misdemeanor restriction; designated courts authorize interception and decide suppression. Section 30-12-11 separately authorizes the affected person’s civil action.
penalties: Unlawful interference under 30-12-1 is a misdemeanor. Civil relief under 30-12-11 includes actual damages with a minimum of $100 per violation day or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus punitive damages and reasonable attorney fees/litigation costs. Good-faith reliance on an order or the Act is a complete defense; compliant carriers also receive specified protection.
deadlines: An interception order lasts only as long as needed, at most 30 days; separately justified extensions each have the same 30-day ceiling. Execution must minimize interception and stop once its objective is met. Parties ordinarily receive the order/application at least 10 days before evidentiary use; a judicial waiver requires impossibility and no prejudice. Suppression motions ordinarily precede the proceeding; specified state appeals have a 30-day deadline.
exemptions: Section 30-12-1(C) uses consent of a sender or intended recipient. Exceptions include a valid interception order, necessary normal-course carrier work, and crime-investigating officials who participate or have a party’s prior consent. These conditional exceptions do not authorize indiscriminate monitoring.
amendments: The 2025 reproduction lists 1973 Chapter 369 §1 and 1979 Chapter 191 §1 as amendments to 30-12-1; the reviewed procedural/civil sections trace to 1973 Chapter 369. The full 2026 enacted-session comparison and original commencement dates are not certified.

title: Insurance Disclosure and Marketing Privacy
summary: Limits insurance-record disclosure, including marketing transfers, and provides targeted remedies.
scope: Insurance institutions, agents and support organizations collecting or keeping information about Ohio natural persons or conducting insurance transactions with Ohio residents. Residency is determined by the last known mailing address in their records.
rights: Individuals can decline the specific marketing-transfer route in 3904.13(K). A person harmed by a prohibited disclosure can recover actual damages under 3904.21.
obligations: Disclosure requires written authorization or a specific statutory exception. Under the marketing exception, recipients must use information only for marketing, individuals must have an opportunity to object, and medical, privileged, character, habit, lifestyle and reputation information and derived classifications cannot be shared.
enacted: Current official historical versions attribute these sections to 120th General Assembly HouseBill 329; the reviewed pages establish the operative 1995 version, rather than its signing day.
effective: The reviewed 1995 sections became effective June 29, 1995. The current 3904.13 disclosure section incorporates 133rd General Assembly SenateBill 9, effective July 1, 2021.
authority: The Superintendent of Insurance may examine and investigate insurers, agents and support organizations, including support activity outside Ohio affecting an Ohio resident. Courts handle the private claims authorized by 3904.21.
penalties: After a hearing finding a knowing violation, up to $500 per violation and $10,000 aggregate. Violating a cease-and-desist order can result in up to $10,000 per violation, or $50,000 for a general business practice, and license suspension/revocation. Section 3904.21 caps private disclosure compensation at actual damages; prevailing-party costs and reasonable attorney fees are discretionary.
deadlines: Private actions must be brought within two years after the violation was or should have been discovered. The marketing-disclosure exception requires an opportunity to object before its use; it supplies no universal fixed-day response clock.
exemptions: Separate conditional routes cover necessary servicing, fraud prevention, regulators, legal process, research and business transfers. Affiliate insurance marketing has its own conditions. Compliant disclosures receive specified defamation/privacy/negligence immunity, but knowingly injurious false information does not.
amendments: The current official 3904.13 page identifies 2021 SenateBill 9 as its latest amendment and supplies the prior June 29, 1995 version. The other reviewed enforcement sections list 1995 HouseBill 329. Every earlier enactment and implementing-rule amendment is outside this bounded section review.

title: Life, Health and Disability Insurance Disclosure Privacy
summary: Restricts insurance-information disclosure and provides a choice against specified marketing transfers.
scope: Life, health and disability insurance institutions, representatives and support organizations handling information or insurance transactions involving Massachusetts residents. Residency follows the last known mailing address in their records. This chapter is not assumed to cover every property/casualty transaction.
rights: Individuals can object to the marketing-transfer route in section 13(11). Section 20 permits special and compensatory damages for prohibited disclosures and equitable relief for violations of the separate access, correction and underwriting-information rights.
obligations: The marketing exception requires an opportunity to object and a promise of marketing-only use. It cannot disclose medical, privileged, health, character, habit, lifestyle or reputation information or classifications derived from them.
enacted: 1991 Chapter 516 §1, approved January 7, 1992, as printed at the end of the original official chapter. The session-law year 1991 is distinct from the January 1992 approval date.
effective: July 1, 1992, expressly stated in original Chapter 516 §3. Section 4 excludes property/casualty insurers and their representatives from the act’s scope.

title: Genetic Testing Privacy in Employment
summary: Restricts employers’ use of private genetic information in hiring, promotion and retention decisions.
scope: Covers employers with five or more employees, including state and local government, as defined in section 39-8302. Protected information includes specified inherited-gene/DNA-marker information about an identifiable person or blood relative. It is an employment-specific protection, not a general consumer genetic-data deletion or broker-registration law.
rights: Covered employment decisions must not use private genetic information, require a genetic test or release, or ask whether a person or blood relative took or refused testing.
obligations: Keep genetic-test requests, releases, access and consideration out of covered employment decisions unless a statutory exception applies. A permitted court order must restrict the information and recipients and include protective measures.
exemptions: Court-compelled disclosure requires an employment proceeding in which health is at issue or a reasonable basis for a real and unjustifiable safety risk, plus unavailable/ineffective alternatives and a compelling need outweighing privacy harm. Forensic or human-remains laboratories may request employee/contractor identification markers solely for contamination quality control. Routine examinations, routine blood/urine analyses, drug/HIV tests and tests prompted by manifested disease are excluded from the defined genetic information.
deadlines: The restrictions apply when making covered employment decisions. Sections 39-8303–8304 do not establish a consumer request-response period or a separate breach-notification deadline; the law is not a time-limited consent-request scheme.
authority: Idaho Attorney General brings the chapter’s specified public enforcement action in court.
penalties: Section 39-8304 authorizes declaratory and injunctive relief, actual damages or restitution on behalf of the state and its agencies, and civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation plus reasonable investigative expenses and attorney fees. Civil penalties go to the general fund. These are public remedies, not an automatic payment to each employee; the section does not itself give an individual a damages action, and preserves other available remedies.
effective: July 1, 2006, reported in the contemporaneous Idaho Hospital Association legislative report filed in the Secretary of State’s lobbying archive.
amendments: Section 39-8303’s history identifies 2022 Chapter 141 section 1, adding the forensic/human-remains laboratory quality-control exception. Section 39-8302 definitions were revised by 2024 Chapter 318; that chapter separately added genetic-sequencer restrictions in section 39-8305, which are not generalized into an employer right to use genetic information.

title: Employee Medical Examinations and Confidential Files
summary: Restricts disability-related employment inquiries and requires separate confidential medical files.
scope: Chapter 5 covered entities include employers engaged in commerce with at least 15 employees for 20 calendar weeks in the current or preceding year; it is not the general six-worker civil-rights threshold. Federal government, Indian tribes and qualifying private membership clubs are excluded by §10.
rights: Protection against prohibited medical inquiries and improper disclosure of covered medical histories.
obligations: Keep post-offer examination and voluntary employee-health-program medical information on separate forms and in separate confidential medical files. Pre-offer disability inquiries are restricted; employee examinations must be job-related and consistent with business necessity.
exemptions: Limited disclosures permit necessary accommodation/work restrictions to supervisors, emergency-treatment information to first-aid/safety staff, and relevant compliance information to government investigators. Illegal-drug testing is not a medical examination under §24.

title: Stop Harms from Addictive Social Media Act
summary: Requires privacy settings, parental consent and limits on addictive or profile-based features for covered child accounts.
scope: Platforms and related entities collectively generating at least $1 billion worldwide advertising revenue in any of the preceding 3 years. A child is an Idaho resident age 16or younger; separate minor-account termination provisions also apply.
rights: Parental consent for a child’s account and changed terms; most-private default settings; no profile-based advertising or addictive interface features for children. Covered personal information includes identifying biometric data and location information.
obligations: Use reasonable age estimates after usage triggers. Limit parental-consent information to that purpose and delete it immediately after the attempt, except legally required retention. Provide parental controls and clear account-termination requests.
deadlines: Initial/revised age estimates within 14 days after 25/50 hours of use within 6 months; later updates each additional 100 hours or more frequently when other demographic analytics update. Minor termination requests: 7 days for the holder,14 for a parent. Age-classification notices: 7 days; dispute window 30 days; determination within 30 days after verification, then termination within 7 days. Damages actions: 3 years from actual/reasonably expected knowledge of the violation.
exemptions: No age-estimation or other action duty under this chapter for accounts continuously held at least 7 years. Broadband and exclusively private messaging services are excluded. Reasonable compliance efforts form a liability defense. The age-estimation section itself requires no new information collection.
authority: AttorneyGeneral under the Consumer Protection Act for knowing/reckless violations; children and parents have an express private action.
penalties: Private relief includes injunction/declaration, damages, costs and reasonable fees. Reckless/knowing violations permit the greater of actual damages or $10,000 statutory damages; a consistent pattern may support punitive damages. Unconsented child-account contracts and waivers have the statutory invalidity rules. AG remedies arise through chapter 6: §48-606 permits injunctions, restitution, costs/fees and civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation; that is distinct from the private $10,000 reckless/knowing-damages floor.

title: Data Security for Money Transmitters Act
summary: Requires licensed money transmitters and virtual-currency kiosks to safeguard customer information and report covered incidents to the banking commissioner.
scope: Money transmitters and virtual-currency kiosks licensed under the Money Transmission Modernization Act. Covers nonpublic customer financial information in paper, electronic or other form maintained by or for a licensee or its affiliates; the Act distinguishes consumers from customers with continuing relationships.
rights: Customers benefit from mandatory security safeguards, limited access and secure disposal. Section 5 requires notice to the banking commissioner; it is not itself a promise of a direct 72-hour notice to every affected customer or a new general consumer deletion right.
obligations: Maintain a written security program scaled to size, complexity, activities and data sensitivity; appoint a qualified individual; assess risks; control access; encrypt information at rest and across external networks, subject to approved compensating controls where infeasible; use multifactor authentication or written approval of equivalent or stronger controls. Train staff, oversee service providers contractually, monitor safeguards and maintain business-continuity/disaster-recovery plans. Maintain incident-response plans and annual leadership reports when required. Dispose of customer information within two years after its last use to provide a financial product or service, subject to the statutory retention exceptions.
exemptions: Licensees maintaining information concerning fewer than 5,000 consumers are excused only from §4(2)(b), (5)(b), (9) and (10): specified written-risk-assessment elements, periodic-testing requirements, the written incident-response plan and annual leadership reporting. Other security and notification duties remain. Disposal may be delayed for legitimate business/operational needs, legally required retention or when targeted disposal is not reasonably feasible because of the storage method.
deadlines: Notify the Commissioner of Banking and Consumer Finance as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after discovering a covered notification event involving a Mississippi consumer. Knowledge of employees, officers or agents counts, excluding the person committing the event. For a service-provider system, the deadline calculation starts the day after provider notification or the licensee’s actual knowledge, whichever is sooner. Annual penetration testing and vulnerability assessments at least every six months apply where the specified periodic-testing regime is required and effective continuous monitoring is absent. A law-enforcement request can delay public disclosure initially up to 30 days and by written extension up to 60 more; it does not erase the commissioner-notice requirement.
authority: Commissioner of Banking and Consumer Finance may examine and investigate covered licensees and take necessary or appropriate enforcement action under §7, in addition to powers under the Money Transmission Modernization Act.
penalties: Sections 1–7 authorize commissioner investigation and enforcement but do not specify a separate dollar fine or create an express private damages action. Existing licensing/enforcement powers are preserved; this record does not invent an automatic per-customer award.
